questions.hint: When Claude outputs both text and tool_use, wait for tool results before returning text to users.

questions.scenario: An agent built with the Claude Agent SDK pulls shipment data from three MCP tools. One returns dates as Unix timestamps, one as ISO 8601 strings, and one as "MM/DD/YYYY". The agent sometimes misorders shipments when it compares dates across tools. The team cannot change the MCP servers this quarter.
questions.question: What is the most reliable way to fix the comparisons?

options.text: Add a PostToolUse hook that rewrites each tool's dates into one format.
Tell the agent in its system prompt to convert every date to ISO 8601.
Add a PreToolUse hook that converts the dates found in each tool's output.
Ask Claude to show its date conversions so reviewers can catch mistakes.

explanation.correct: A PostToolUse hook runs after a tool returns and before Claude sees the result. By returning updatedToolOutput it can replace the output with a normalized version, so every date reaches the model in one format, deterministically and without changing the servers.

distractors.B: The model would have to convert correctly on every call. That is probabilistic, and it is the kind of mistake the team is already seeing.
distractors.C: PreToolUse runs before the tool executes, when there is no output yet. It can change the tool's input but not its result.
distractors.D: Showing conversions makes mistakes visible but does not prevent them, and it depends on a human reviewing every run.

questions.hint: The loop should check stop_reason after each response to decide whether to run tools or return final text.

questions.scenario: A cloud-operations agent can call a delete_resource MCP tool. The team must make sure the agent never deletes a resource tagged env=production, while still letting it clean up staging resources on its own. When a production deletion is requested, the change should go through the team's change-request process instead.
questions.question: Which approach meets these requirements?

options.text: A PostToolUse hook that logs every deletion and pages the on-call engineer at once.
A system prompt rule saying production resources must never be deleted.
A PreToolUse hook that denies production deletions and names the change process.
Removing the delete_resource tool from the agent's tool set entirely.

explanation.correct: A PreToolUse hook runs before the call executes. It can check the resource's tag and return a deny decision whose reason points Claude to the change-request process. Production deletions are blocked deterministically, staging cleanup still works, and Claude receives the reason and can redirect.

distractors.A: PostToolUse runs after the tool has executed, so the production resource is already gone when anyone is alerted.
distractors.B: A prompt rule is probabilistic guidance, but the requirement is that the deletion never happens.
distractors.D: Removing the tool blocks production deletions but also blocks the staging cleanup the agent is supposed to do.

questions.hint: Use pre-tool-use hooks to enforce policies before Claude can call tools - they inspect the planned call and deny if needed.

questions.scenario: A team plans to use a PreToolUse hook to deny tool calls that break a data-export policy. One engineer worries that a denial in the middle of a long run will crash the agent or end the session, and proposes letting the call run and cleaning up afterward instead.
questions.question: What happens when the hook denies a call, and what should the team decide?

options.text: The session ends with an error, so the team should clean up after the call.
The call doesn't run and Claude gets the reason, so denying is safe to use.
The call runs but its output is hidden, so the team should add a second hook.
Claude receives nothing and retries forever, so the team should cap retries.

explanation.correct: A denied call does not execute. Claude receives the denial, including the hook's reason, as the tool result, and usually tries another approach or explains that it cannot proceed. Blocking up front is safer than letting a policy-violating call run.

distractors.A: A denial does not end the session. The loop continues with the rejection as the tool result.
distractors.C: A denied call never executes, so there is no output to hide. A second hook would solve a problem that does not exist.
distractors.D: Claude receives the rejection message as the tool result, so it is not left waiting with nothing.

questions.hint: A deny behavior in hooks blocks tool use entirely - useful for security policies that should never be bypassed.

questions.scenario: An Agent SDK app registers a PreToolUse hook with the matcher "Write|Edit". The hook denies any call whose file_path is inside the secrets/ directory. During a red-team test, the agent still created a file in secrets/ by running a shell command through the Bash tool.
questions.question: What should the team do?

options.text: Change the matcher to "secrets/*" so the hook fires for any secrets path.
Add a PostToolUse hook on Write and Edit that deletes files in secrets/.
Add a line to the system prompt telling the agent never to touch secrets/.
Also cover Bash, by checking its commands in a hook or by sandbox rules.

explanation.correct: Matchers filter on tool name, so a Write|Edit hook never sees Bash calls, a gap the documentation warns about. Protection must cover every tool that can write: a Bash-matched hook that inspects the command, or sandbox rules that restrict what Bash can write.

distractors.A: Matchers match tool names, not file paths or other arguments, so a "secrets/*" matcher would never match any tool.
distractors.B: This still misses Bash, and deleting files after they are written is cleanup, not prevention.
distractors.C: A prompt line is probabilistic, and the red-team test already got around the agent's intended behavior.

questions.hint: Hook matchers route tool calls to different policies; comprehensive coverage means every tool has an appropriate matcher.

questions.scenario: Every month, a compliance team asks an agent to review about 40 supplier contracts. Each contract always gets the same five checks in the same order: parties, term, liability cap, data-protection clause, and termination rights. The checks and their order have not changed in two years.
questions.question: Which decomposition pattern fits this workflow?

options.text: A fixed prompt chain that runs the five checks in order on each contract.
Dynamic decomposition where the agent plans new subtasks for each contract.
One prompt that applies all five checks to all 40 contracts at once.
A separate agent per contract with the open-ended goal of finding issues.

explanation.correct: When the steps are known and stable, prompt chaining gives predictable, repeatable results. Each step focuses on one check, and the same chain runs for every contract.

distractors.B: Dynamic decomposition suits open-ended work where later steps depend on what is found. Here it adds variation to a process that should run the same way every time.
distractors.C: Packing 40 contracts and five checks into one pass invites diluted attention and missed clauses.
distractors.D: An open-ended goal drops the defined checklist, so checks may be skipped or applied differently from contract to contract.

sources: Design guidance, not a claim from Anthropic docs (checked 2026-11-07)
questions.hint: Prompt chaining breaks complex tasks into sequential subprompts - each handles one concern at a time.

questions.scenario: A team asks Claude Code to "add meaningful tests to our 8-year-old billing service," which has almost no tests today. The codebase has about 300 files, and nobody on the team fully understands its dependencies. A first attempt wrote tests file by file in alphabetical order and spent most of its effort on rarely used utilities.
questions.question: How should this task be decomposed?

options.text: Write tests file by file again, but work through them in reverse alphabetical order.
Ask for tests for every file in one prompt so nothing is left out.
Map the structure, rank high-impact areas, then plan tests that adapt as you go.
Generate tests only for the 20 largest files, since size predicts risk.

explanation.correct: Open-ended work on an unfamiliar codebase calls for adaptive decomposition: understand the structure first, focus on the code that matters most, such as billing calculations and payment paths, and adjust the plan as dependencies come to light.

distractors.A: Changing the order does not address the problem, because the order still has nothing to do with importance.
distractors.B: A single prompt across 300 files gives no prioritization and cannot hold the context any one area needs.
distractors.D: File size is a weak proxy for risk, and small files often hold critical logic.

sources: Design guidance, not a claim from Anthropic docs (checked 2026-11-07)
questions.hint: Adaptive decomposition adjusts task breakdown based on what it learns - prioritize complex subtasks when needed.

questions.scenario: An on-call agent investigates production incidents. The team has a standard runbook chain: check recent deploys, then error rates, then database health, then roll back the latest deploy. Most incidents last quarter were novel failures whose cause emerged only after following clues across services, and the fixed chain often ended in an unnecessary rollback.
questions.question: How should the investigation be structured?

options.text: Keep the fixed runbook chain and add two more steps at the end of it.
Start from the symptoms and pick each next step from what has been found.
Run every diagnostic check in parallel and send all the output to the engineer.
Skip the investigation and always roll back the latest deploy straight away.

explanation.correct: When each step depends on what the previous one revealed, dynamic decomposition fits better than a fixed chain. The agent forms and revises a plan as clues appear, instead of running a sequence that ends in a rollback whatever the cause.

distractors.A: A fixed chain is defensible for repeatable checks, but these incidents were mostly novel. A longer chain still cannot follow clues.
distractors.C: Running everything gives breadth without reasoning and leaves the engineer to correlate a flood of output.
distractors.D: Always rolling back ignores the evidence that most causes were not recent deploys.

sources: Design guidance, not a claim from Anthropic docs (checked 2026-11-07)
questions.hint: Dynamic decomposition creates prompts on the fly based on context, trading specificity for flexibility.

questions.scenario: A platform team is deciding which of its agent workflows to build as fixed prompt chains and which as dynamic, adaptive plans.
questions.question: Which two workflows are the best fit for a fixed prompt chain? (Select two.)

options.text: A weekly SLA summary built from the same three dashboards in the same format.
Debugging an intermittent failure that shows up only under heavy production load.
Answering "where is authorization enforced?" in an unfamiliar codebase.
Translating release notes, then applying the style guide, then a glossary check.
Investigating why customer churn jumped last month across several regions.

explanation.correct: Both workflows have known, stable steps that do not depend on intermediate findings. That is what prompt chaining handles well: predictable output, with each step focused on one job.

distractors.B: Intermittent failures need hypotheses that change with each finding, which calls for dynamic decomposition.
distractors.C: Exploring unfamiliar code means following imports and call paths as they are discovered, so the steps cannot be fixed in advance.
distractors.E: A churn investigation branches on what the data shows, such as region, segment, or pricing changes, so it needs an adaptive plan.

sources: Design guidance, not a claim from Anthropic docs (checked 2026-11-07)
questions.hint: Choose prompt chaining for predictable steps, dynamic for context-driven complexity in the decomposition.

questions.scenario: Yesterday a developer used an Agent SDK session to analyze a payments module in depth. Overnight, teammates merged a refactor that rewrote about 60% of the module's files and renamed several core classes. Today the developer wants to continue the work with an agent.
questions.question: What is the best way to start today's work?

options.text: Resume yesterday's session and continue without mentioning the refactor.
Fork yesterday's session so the original analysis stays safe.
Start a new session with a short summary of yesterday's conclusions.
Resume yesterday's session and send /compact before the next prompt.

explanation.correct: Resuming restores the earlier tool results, and most of them now describe code that no longer exists. With most of the module rewritten, a fresh session seeded with a structured summary of what still holds is more reliable than a resumed context full of stale file contents.

distractors.A: The resumed agent would reason from outdated file contents and class names, and could give confident answers about code that has changed.
distractors.B: A fork copies the same stale history. It protects the old analysis but does not fix the starting point for new work.
distractors.D: Compaction summarizes the stale content instead of removing it, so the outdated picture carries forward in compressed form.

questions.hint: Session resumption reloads prior context to continue work, avoiding the need to recompute state from scratch.

questions.scenario: An agent session has spent an hour mapping a legacy codebase. The developer now wants to compare two refactoring strategies, each explored from that same analysis, without either exploration affecting the other and without repeating the hour of mapping.
questions.question: Which approach fits?

options.text: Resume the original session twice in a row, exploring one strategy each time.
Start two new sessions and let each one map the codebase again.
Use continue mode so the SDK picks up the most recent session.
Fork the session for one strategy and continue the original for the other.

explanation.correct: Forking creates a new session that starts with a copy of the original history and then diverges, while the original stays unchanged, so each strategy builds on the shared analysis independently. Forking branches only the conversation: file edits made in one branch are still visible to the other.

distractors.A: Both resumes add to the same history, so the second exploration sees the first one's reasoning.
distractors.B: This keeps the explorations independent but throws away an hour of analysis and pays for it twice.
distractors.C: Continue resumes the most recent session and adds to it, giving one shared history rather than two branches.

questions.hint: Session forking creates parallel branches from a checkpoint, allowing exploration without losing the original.

questions.scenario: On Monday, an agent session analyzed a 40-file reporting service. On Tuesday, a teammate changed the signatures of two functions in report_builder.py and nothing else. The developer resumes Monday's session, and the agent keeps suggesting calls that use the old signatures.
questions.question: What should the developer do?

options.text: Start a new session and have the agent explore all 40 files again from scratch.
Tell the resumed session which file changed so it re-reads that file.
Fork the session and continue the work in the fork instead of the original.
Send /compact so the agent forgets the old signatures it read on Monday.

explanation.correct: Almost all of Monday's context is still valid, so resuming makes sense. The agent only needs to know what changed, and naming the changed file leads to a targeted re-read instead of a full re-exploration.

distractors.A: Starting fresh throws away analysis that is still almost entirely valid. That is the right call when most of the context is stale, which is not the case here.
distractors.C: A fork copies the same outdated view of report_builder.py, so the stale signatures carry over.
distractors.D: Compaction summarizes history rather than refreshing it, so the old signatures may survive in the summary.

questions.hint: Targeted reanalysis revisits specific questions from a session, using current context and tools as needed.

questions.scenario: A finance assistant has a get_invoice tool that returns one invoice from the billing system by its ID (format INV-123456), including line items, totals, and dates. It does not return payment status; a separate get_payment_status tool does that. The team is writing the description for get_invoice.
questions.question: Which description will help Claude choose and call the tool most reliably?

options.text: Gets an invoice.
Returns one invoice by ID (INV-123456): line items, totals, dates. Use when the user names an invoice. For payment status, use get_payment_status.
A powerful general billing tool. Use it whenever the conversation mentions billing, invoices, payments, refunds, or money in any form, so the user always gets an answer.
Calls GET /v2/billing/invoices/{id} on the internal billing service with a five-second timeout, three retries with backoff, and JSON response parsing.

explanation.correct: A good description says what the tool does, what it returns, when to use it, what the input means, and what it does not cover, with a pointer to the right tool for that. That is what Claude uses to choose between similar tools.

distractors.A: A one-line description leaves Claude guessing about the input format, the output, and the boundary with get_payment_status.
distractors.C: Over-broad trigger words route payment questions to the wrong tool. A description should narrow when the tool applies, not widen it.
distractors.D: Implementation details such as endpoints and retries do not help Claude decide when to call the tool or what it gets back.

questions.hint: When selecting tools, use clear descriptions that differentiate each tool's purpose and output.

questions.scenario: A support agent has two tools: get_contact, which reads the sales CRM, and lookup_user, which reads accounts in the product database. Both descriptions say "Finds a person by name or email." When users report login problems, the agent often calls get_contact and then reports that it can't see any login history.
questions.question: What is the most effective fix?

options.text: Add a line to the system prompt telling Claude to think carefully about which tool to call.
Remove lookup_user and ask users to provide their CRM contact ID instead.
Add input_examples to both tools showing typical names and email addresses.
Prefix the names by system (crm_, app_) and describe what each returns and when to use it.

explanation.correct: The two tools overlap in name and description, so Claude has nothing to tell them apart. Naming each tool after its service and describing what it returns (CRM contact data vs product account and login data) and when to use it removes the ambiguity at its source.

distractors.A: A general "think carefully" instruction gives Claude no new information about the difference between the tools.
distractors.B: Removing the tool that has the login data makes the login questions impossible to answer.
distractors.C: Examples of names and emails show the input format, which both tools share. They say nothing about which system each tool reads.

questions.hint: Avoid tool name collisions by designing distinct names or splitting overlapping tools.

questions.scenario: An order-management agent has well-described tools, including get_order_history and cancel_order. Its system prompt says: "Whenever the user mentions an order, always check their order history first." When a user writes "Cancel order 5521", the agent spends several turns reading order history before cancelling, and sometimes asks the user to confirm details they already gave.
questions.question: What should the team change?

options.text: Narrow the system prompt rule so not every mention of an order goes to history.
Make the cancel_order description longer than the get_order_history description.
Add a third tool that calls order history and then cancels the order in a single step.
Remove get_order_history so the agent cannot read history before cancelling.

explanation.correct: A keyword-triggered rule in the system prompt ("whenever the user mentions an order") overrides the tool descriptions, so a clear cancel request still goes through order history. Narrowing the rule to the cases that need history lets the descriptions do their job.

distractors.B: Description length is not a priority signal. The system prompt rule still tells Claude to read history first.
distractors.C: A combined tool works around the rule for one case and adds a tool that overlaps both existing ones.
distractors.D: Order history is needed for other questions, and the rule would still push the agent toward a tool that no longer exists.

questions.hint: Tools must work WITH system prompts - clarify expectations rather than conflict.

questions.scenario: An agent integrates with an issue tracker through 14 separate tools: create_issue, close_issue, reopen_issue, label_issue, unlabel_issue, assign_issue, unassign_issue, and seven more of the same kind. Each tool is described accurately, but Claude often picks a neighbor of the right tool, such as unlabel_issue when it meant label_issue.
questions.question: What change best improves tool selection?

options.text: Split the tools further, so each one covers a single field change on a single issue type.
Keep all 14 tools and add input_examples to every one of them.
Merge them into one issue tool with a described action parameter.
Remove the seven least-used operations and handle them manually outside the agent.

explanation.correct: Many near-identical tools make selection harder, not easier. Grouping related operations into one tool with an action parameter (an enum, with each action described) reduces the choice to one tool and one clearly listed option, which current guidance recommends for exactly this situation.

distractors.A: Splitting further multiplies the near-identical choices that are causing the errors. Splitting helps when one tool hides several different input and output contracts, which is not the case here.
distractors.B: Examples show input formats. They do not reduce the number of similar tools Claude has to choose between.
distractors.D: Dropping operations removes functionality users need, and the remaining seven tools are still near-duplicates of each other.

questions.hint: Consolidate overlapping tools to reduce choice complexity and improve reliability.

questions.scenario: A document agent has one process_document tool with a mode parameter: "extract" returns JSON fields, "summarize" returns prose, and "verify" checks a claim against the document and returns a verdict. Each mode uses a different subset of eight optional parameters. Claude often sends parameter combinations that are invalid for the chosen mode.
questions.question: What is the best fix?

options.text: Expand the description to explain which parameters belong to which mode.
Replace it with three tools, each with its own input schema and output contract.
Make all eight parameters required so Claude always provides every value.
Validate the inputs afterwards and ask Claude to retry when a combination is invalid.

explanation.correct: The modes are really three tools with different inputs and outputs hidden behind one schema that cannot express which parameters go together. Separate tools give each operation a schema that only allows valid inputs and a clear output contract.

distractors.A: A longer description helps a little, but the schema still accepts every invalid combination, so errors keep happening.
distractors.C: Requiring all eight parameters forces Claude to invent values that do not apply to the mode.
distractors.D: Retrying after validation catches errors late and costs extra turns, while the schema keeps inviting the same mistakes.

questions.hint: Split complex tools into simpler ones and provide clear parameter descriptions.

questions.scenario: A get_shipment tool returns the full database row for a shipment: about 60 fields, including internal surrogate keys such as row_id and carrier_ref_internal alongside the public tracking number. Claude sometimes quotes row_id to customers as their tracking number.
questions.question: What change addresses this best?

options.text: Raise max_tokens so Claude has more room to process the full response.
Tell Claude in the system prompt to ignore fields that look internal.
Return the raw row and add a short summary of the key fields at the top.
Return only the fields Claude needs, using public, stable identifiers.

explanation.correct: Tool responses should carry high-signal information and semantic, stable identifiers. Returning only the needed fields, with the public tracking number as the identifier, removes the confusing internal keys and saves context.

distractors.A: The problem is which fields come back, not output length. max_tokens limits Claude's response, not the tool result.
distractors.B: A prompt rule relies on Claude recognizing "internal-looking" fields every time, while the confusing data keeps arriving.
distractors.C: A summary helps, but the internal keys are still in the result and can still be quoted.

questions.hint: Design high-signal tool responses - concise structured output, not verbose logs.

questions.scenario: A scheduling tool takes a recurrence parameter in a strict format, such as "FREQ=WEEKLY;BYDAY=MO,WE". Its description explains the tool well, but Claude often produces malformed recurrence strings such as "every Monday and Wednesday", which the backend rejects.
questions.question: What should the team do first?

options.text: Document the format in the parameter description and add input_examples.
Accept free text for recurrence and convert it on the server with regular expressions.
Retry automatically until Claude happens to produce a string the backend accepts.
Remove the recurrence parameter and ask users to set repeating events by hand.

explanation.correct: For format-sensitive parameters, the parameter description plus input_examples show Claude exactly what valid input looks like. Each example must match the schema, so they double as documentation the API checks.

distractors.B: Parsing free text with regular expressions on the server is brittle and moves the ambiguity into code that cannot ask for clarification.
distractors.C: Blind retries cost turns and do not give Claude any new information about the expected format.
distractors.D: Dropping the parameter removes a feature to avoid fixing a documentation problem.

questions.hint: Include input examples and detailed parameter descriptions for Claude to choose right arguments.

questions.scenario: A team is building an MCP server whose search_tickets tool calls an upstream ticketing API. Sometimes that API times out. The team wants the agent to see the failure and decide what to do next, such as retrying or telling the user.
questions.question: How should the MCP server report the timeout?

options.text: Return a normal successful result containing an empty list of tickets.
Return a JSON-RPC protocol error from the tools/call request.
Return a tool result with isError: true and a failure message.
Log the error on the server and return no content to the client.

explanation.correct: The MCP spec reports tool execution failures, such as an upstream API failure, inside the tool result with isError: true. The model sees the message as the tool's output and can decide how to recover.

distractors.A: An empty success says "no tickets match", which is false. The agent would give the user a wrong answer instead of handling an outage.
distractors.B: Protocol errors are for problems with the request itself, such as an unknown tool. The spec puts API failures in the tool result so the model can reason about them.
distractors.D: Returning nothing hides the failure from the agent, which then cannot react to it.

questions.hint: Use isError to catch execution errors and handle unexpected tool response formats.

questions.scenario: Every error from a team's MCP tools returns the same text: "Operation failed." Logs show the agent retrying invalid-input errors five times in a row, while giving up immediately on brief network timeouts that would have succeeded on a second try.
questions.question: What change helps the agent recover appropriately?

options.text: Wrap every tool call in automatic retry logic that retries any error three times.
Return structured errors: a category, an isRetryable flag, a message.
Tell the agent in its prompt never to retry a tool call more than twice.
Return just the HTTP status code from the upstream service as the error text.

explanation.correct: A uniform message hides the one thing the agent needs: whether trying again can help. A category (transient, validation, permission, business), an isRetryable flag, and a readable message let it retry timeouts and fix or report invalid input instead.

distractors.A: Retrying everything wastes calls on errors that will never succeed, such as invalid input, and still gives the agent no explanation.
distractors.C: A fixed cap treats every error the same, so it still under-retries timeouts and over-retries invalid input.
distractors.D: A raw status code is better than nothing, but it lacks a retry hint and a human-readable explanation of what to change.

questions.hint: Distinguish structured errors from retryable errors - handle each type appropriately.

questions.scenario: A hotel-booking agent calls cancel_booking. When a cancellation falls outside the free-cancellation window, the tool returns "Error 422." The agent retries several times, then tells the guest that "a technical problem" stopped the cancellation, which leads to complaints.
questions.question: What should the tool return instead?

options.text: A success result, so the agent stops retrying and moves on to the next request.
A protocol-level error, so the client stops the session and alerts an engineer.
The same 422 code, plus a system prompt rule asking the agent to explain policies.
A non-retryable business-rule error with a guest-friendly explanation.

explanation.correct: This is a business-rule outcome, not a malfunction. Marking it as a non-retryable business error with a guest-friendly explanation (for example, that the window closed 48 hours before check-in) stops the pointless retries and lets the agent tell the guest the real reason and their options.

distractors.A: Reporting success when nothing was cancelled misleads both the agent and the guest.
distractors.B: Stopping the session for a normal policy outcome is far too drastic. The agent should explain and continue.
distractors.C: The agent still cannot tell which policy applied or that retrying is pointless, so it has to guess what to tell the guest.

questions.hint: Business rule errors need different handling than system failures - categorize clearly.

questions.scenario: A customer-lookup tool returns an empty list in two situations: when no customer matches the query, and when the customer database is unreachable. During a database outage, the agent confidently told several callers that they had no account on file.
questions.question: How should the tool change?

options.text: An error result when the lookup fails; an empty success only for no match.
Return an empty list in both cases, but add a note in the system prompt about outages.
Keep the empty list, and retry every empty result three times before answering.
Return a randomly chosen similar customer whenever the database is unreachable.

explanation.correct: An access failure and a valid empty result mean different things and need different responses. Reporting the failure as an error lets the agent say it could not check, while an empty success still means no match.

distractors.B: The agent still cannot tell from the result which situation it is in, so the prompt note cannot help.
distractors.C: Retries add delay to every genuine "no match" result and still cannot tell an outage from no data.
distractors.D: Inventing a match is worse than the original problem. It gives callers someone else's account.

questions.hint: Empty results mean no data; access failures mean permissions - handle them differently.

questions.scenario: In a multi-agent system, an inventory subagent calls an MCP stock-level tool that times out on about 5% of calls; a second attempt almost always succeeds. Today every timeout is passed straight up to the coordinator, which re-plans the whole task. Runs are slow, and the coordinator's context fills with error reports.
questions.question: What is the best design?

options.text: Have the coordinator retry every failed tool call itself, so all recovery stays in one place.
Have the subagent hide timeouts by returning empty stock levels as a successful result.
Retry transient errors in the subagent; escalate the rest with partial results.
Raise the tool timeout to five minutes so that timeouts become much less frequent.

explanation.correct: Transient failures that a retry usually fixes should be handled where they happen. The subagent retries a bounded number of times and passes up only errors it cannot resolve, along with what it tried and any partial results, so the coordinator re-plans only when it needs to.

distractors.A: Centralizing recovery sounds tidy, but it puts every routine timeout through the coordinator, which is exactly what is slowing runs and filling its context.
distractors.B: Reporting a failure as an empty success makes the system act on false stock data.
distractors.D: A huge timeout makes every slow call block for minutes, and the occasional failure still needs handling.

questions.hint: Implement local error recovery with proper error propagation and context.

questions.scenario: A platform team is standardizing the error format that all of its MCP tools return to agents.
questions.question: Which two fields most help an agent decide what to do after a tool error? (Select two.)

options.text: The full server-side stack trace of the exception that was raised.
Whether retrying the same call could succeed, such as an isRetryable flag.
An error category, such as transient, validation, permission, or business.
The hostname and process ID of the particular server instance that handled the call.
The date and time of the server's most recent deployment.

explanation.correct: The agent's next move depends on whether retrying can help and on what kind of problem occurred. A retry flag and a category answer exactly those questions, and a readable message completes the picture.

distractors.A: Stack traces are useful to engineers but noisy for the agent, and they can leak internal details.
distractors.D: Host and process details help operators debug, not the agent deciding its next step.
distractors.E: Deployment timing has no bearing on how the agent should respond to this call.

questions.hint: Let prompts help Claude search locally when it cannot find what it needs.

questions.scenario: A single operations agent has 22 tools from five integrations: monitoring, ticketing, deployments, chat, and billing. As tools were added, the rate of wrong-tool calls rose steadily, even though each tool is well described.
questions.question: What change is most likely to restore reliable tool selection?

options.text: Add input_examples to all 22 tools so every tool's usage is clearer.
Add a long section to the system prompt explaining when to use each of the 22 tools.
Switch to a larger model and keep the same 22 tools on the one agent.
Split into specialist subagents, each with only the tools its role needs.

explanation.correct: Giving one agent many tools increases decision complexity and degrades selection. Specialist subagents with small, role-specific tool sets (for example, incident triage with monitoring and ticketing tools) each face far fewer choices.

distractors.A: Examples clarify inputs, but the agent still chooses among 22 tools on every turn.
distractors.B: More prompt text about 22 tools adds context without reducing the number of choices.
distractors.C: A larger model may help a little, but the choice among 22 tools stays just as complex.

questions.hint: Constrained tools force Claude down paths - scope tools to correct contexts.

questions.scenario: A help-center agent has a generic fetch_url tool so it can read the company documentation site. Logs show it sometimes fetches arbitrary external pages and, once, an internal admin URL that appeared in a user's message. It only ever needs published documentation articles.
questions.question: What is the best change?

options.text: Add a system prompt rule saying the agent may only fetch documentation pages.
Replace fetch_url with load_doc, which takes a published document ID.
Keep fetch_url, and review a weekly log of every URL the agent fetched.
List the allowed documentation URLs in the system prompt for the agent to check.

explanation.correct: A constrained tool that accepts a document ID, and only loads published docs, removes the ability to reach anything else and gives Claude a simpler input. The agent cannot fetch an admin URL because the tool cannot express one.

distractors.A: A prompt rule is guidance, not a guarantee, and the admin-URL incident shows instructions can be steered by user input.
distractors.C: A weekly review finds problems after the data has already been fetched.
distractors.D: The agent still holds a general fetch tool, and checking a list is something it can skip or get wrong.

questions.hint: Constrained tools work well for narrow, specific tasks - design accordingly.

questions.scenario: A document-intake pipeline runs on Claude Opus 5 with three extraction tools: extract_invoice, extract_receipt, and extract_contract. The document type is not known in advance. With the default tool_choice, Claude occasionally replies with a prose summary instead of calling any tool, which breaks the pipeline.
questions.question: Which tool_choice setting fits?

options.text: {"type": "auto"}, together with a stronger instruction in the system prompt.
{"type": "tool", "name": "extract_invoice"} on every request.
{"type": "any"}, so Claude must call one of the tools but picks which.
{"type": "none"}, and parse the JSON out of Claude's prose reply.

explanation.correct: On models that support forced tool use, such as Claude Opus 5, "any" guarantees a tool call while leaving the choice of tool to Claude, which is what you want when the document type is unknown.

distractors.A: auto lets Claude answer in prose, which is the failure being fixed. A prompt instruction makes a tool call more likely but not certain.
distractors.B: Forcing extract_invoice would run invoice extraction on receipts and contracts too.
distractors.D: none disables tool use entirely, giving up the schema-validated output the pipeline relies on.

questions.hint: Use tool_choice to enforce tool use when needed, but balance against flexibility.

questions.scenario: A team moves an extraction pipeline from Claude Opus 5 to Claude Opus 5.5. The pipeline sets tool_choice to {"type": "any"} so that Claude always calls one of its extraction tools. On Claude Opus 5.5, every request now fails with a 400 error.
questions.question: What should the team do?

options.text: Use auto with an instruction to call a tool, set strict: true, and retry if no tool is called.
Keep "any" in the request, catch the 400 error, and resend the same request after a short delay.
Set tool_choice to none and ask Claude to write the extracted JSON as plain text.
Switch to {"type": "tool", "name": ...} so the request names one specific tool to call.

explanation.correct: Claude Opus 5.5 rejects forced tool use: both "any" and "tool" return a 400. The documented replacement is auto with an explicit instruction, strict: true on the tools to keep schema-valid inputs, and a check that a call was made, with a retry if not. Structured outputs are the other option when the call only existed to get JSON back.

distractors.B: The 400 is a fixed rule for this model, not a temporary error, so resending the same request fails every time.
distractors.C: none disables tools, and free-text JSON gives up the schema guarantees the pipeline relied on.
distractors.D: Naming a specific tool is also forced tool use, which this model rejects in the same way.

questions.hint: Model differences mean strict tool use may not work equally - test across supported models.

questions.scenario: A pipeline on Claude Opus 5 must always start by calling extract_metadata on each document. After that first step, Claude should decide on its own which of several enrichment tools, if any, to call next.
questions.question: How should tool_choice be set?

options.text: {"type": "any"} on every request, so Claude always calls one of the tools.
Force extract_metadata on the first request, then use auto on the turns after it.
Force extract_metadata on every request until the document has been fully processed.
Leave auto throughout, and list extract_metadata first in the tools array.

explanation.correct: Naming the tool in tool_choice on the first request guarantees that step runs first. Switching to auto afterwards returns the choice of enrichment tools, including whether to call any, to Claude.

distractors.A: "any" does not guarantee extract_metadata comes first, and it forces a tool call even when no enrichment is needed.
distractors.C: Forcing extract_metadata on every turn stops Claude from ever calling the enrichment tools.
distractors.D: The order of tools in the array is not a control mechanism, so Claude may skip the metadata step.

questions.hint: Structure prompts to maintain clear context flow when tools depend on previous results.

questions.scenario: On Claude Opus 5, a team forces a specific diagnosis tool with tool_choice so that it is always called. They notice the tool is called with shallow arguments, and responses never include any thinking before the call. They want Claude to reason first and still call the tool.
questions.question: What should they change?

options.text: Keep forcing the tool and raise max_tokens so there is room for reasoning.
Switch to {"type": "any"} so Claude has a choice among the tools.
Use auto and tell Claude in the prompt to use the diagnosis tool.
Set tool_choice to none and describe the diagnosis tool in the system prompt.

explanation.correct: A forced tool call skips thinking: the response starts with the tool_use block. Using auto, with a prompt instruction naming the tool, lets Claude think before making the call, while prompting still steers which tool it picks.

distractors.A: More output room does not change the fact that a forced call skips thinking.
distractors.B: "any" is also forced tool use, so the call still skips thinking.
distractors.D: none prevents the tool from being called at all.

questions.hint: High-signal output means Claude gives what you need without asking - design for efficiency.

questions.scenario: A team wants every developer to get the same Jira MCP server in Claude Code as soon as they clone or pull the repository, with no manual setup beyond their own credentials.
questions.question: Where should the server be configured?

options.text: In project scope, in a .mcp.json file at the repository root.
In user scope, in each developer's own ~/.claude.json.
In local scope, on the machine of the developer who set it up.
In the project's CLAUDE.md, as a description of the server.

explanation.correct: Project scope stores the server in .mcp.json at the project root, which is committed to version control, so everyone who clones the repository gets it.

distractors.B: User scope applies to one developer across their projects and is not shared through the repository.
distractors.C: Local scope is private to one developer in one project, so teammates never see it.
distractors.D: CLAUDE.md holds instructions and context. Describing a server there does not configure or connect it.

questions.hint: Scoped tool access with project scope keeps context contained and clean.

questions.scenario: A project's .mcp.json configures a GitHub MCP server, and a developer pasted a personal access token directly into the headers field. The team wants to keep the shared configuration in the repository without committing anyone's secret.
questions.question: What should they do?

options.text: Keep the token in the file but make the repository private.
Use ${GITHUB_TOKEN} in the file; each developer sets the variable.
Move the server to user scope on every developer's machine instead.
Base64-encode the token so it is not readable in the committed file.

explanation.correct: .mcp.json supports environment variable expansion (${VAR}, or ${VAR:-default}) in fields such as headers, url, and env. The committed file holds only the reference, and each developer supplies their own token through the environment.

distractors.A: A private repository still exposes the secret to everyone with access, and to its full history.
distractors.C: User scope avoids committing the token but gives up the shared, version-controlled configuration the team wants.
distractors.D: Base64 is an encoding, not encryption. Anyone can decode the token.

questions.hint: Credential management requires explicit tool setup - don't rely on defaults.

questions.scenario: A developer wants to try an experimental MCP server while working on one particular project. It should not appear in their other projects, and teammates should never see it.
questions.question: Which scope fits?

options.text: Project scope, with a note in .mcp.json saying the server is experimental.
User scope, so the server lives in their own ~/.claude.json file.
A section in the project's CLAUDE.md describing the server.
Local scope, which is private to them and limited to this project.

explanation.correct: Local scope stores the server in ~/.claude.json under that project's path, so it loads only in this project and is never shared through version control.

distractors.A: Project scope commits the server to .mcp.json, so every teammate gets it, whatever the note says.
distractors.B: User scope is private, but it loads in all of the developer's projects, not just this one.
distractors.C: CLAUDE.md does not configure MCP servers.

questions.hint: Local scope prevents unintended access and improves performance - contain tool context.

questions.scenario: An analytics agent uses an MCP server for a data warehouse. Before most queries, it makes a series of exploratory tool calls (listing schemas, listing tables, describing columns) just to find out what data exists, which adds latency and fills context.
questions.question: What change best reduces the exploration?

options.text: Add a list_everything tool that returns every schema, table, and column in one call.
Paste the entire warehouse schema into the agent's system prompt.
Expose the schema catalog as MCP resources that can be referenced when needed.
Raise the agent's turn limit so the exploration has room to finish.

explanation.correct: MCP resources let a server expose content catalogs, such as schemas or documentation, that can be referenced directly (in Claude Code with @server:protocol://path) and are fetched as attachments, so the agent can see what exists without exploratory tool calls.

distractors.A: One giant call still dumps everything into context on every run, most of it irrelevant to the query at hand.
distractors.B: The whole schema in every prompt costs context on every request and goes stale as the warehouse changes.
distractors.D: A higher turn limit accepts the slow exploration instead of removing it.

questions.hint: Use context efficiency with MCP resources - they share the same conversation context.

questions.scenario: A team built an MCP code-search tool that understands symbols across all of the company's repositories. Its description says only "Searches code." Claude keeps using plain text search in the current repository instead, and misses usages in other repositories.
questions.question: What is the most effective fix?

options.text: Describe what it does that text search can't, and when to prefer it.
Remove Bash from the session so that plain text search is no longer available.
Rename the MCP tool to grep so Claude reaches for it out of habit.
Add a system prompt line telling Claude never to use plain text search at all.

explanation.correct: Claude chooses tools from their descriptions. "Searches code" gives no reason to prefer the MCP tool. Explaining that it searches symbols across every repository, and when that beats local text search, lets Claude pick it for the right questions.

distractors.B: Removing Bash takes away far more than text search, and the MCP tool would still be poorly described.
distractors.C: A misleading name confuses selection further and clashes with the familiar meaning of grep.
distractors.D: A blanket ban blocks text search even where it is the right tool, such as quick searches within one file.

questions.hint: Clear tool descriptions prevent wrong choices - specify inputs and outputs precisely.

questions.scenario: A team wants its coding agent to work with Jira, which has a widely used existing MCP server, and with an internal deployment-approval system that only this company uses. An engineer proposes writing custom MCP servers for both, to keep full control.
questions.question: What is the best approach?

options.text: Write custom servers for both, since owning the code gives the team full control.
Use an existing server for Jira; build a custom one for approvals.
Look for existing servers for both systems and skip custom development entirely.
Skip MCP and have the agent call both APIs with curl through the Bash tool.

explanation.correct: Existing servers cover standard integrations and are already maintained. Custom servers are worth building for team-specific systems that nothing else supports. Splitting the work this way minimizes what the team has to build and maintain.

distractors.A: Full control is a real benefit, but rebuilding a standard Jira integration costs time and ongoing maintenance for little gain.
distractors.C: An internal approval system will not have an existing server, so it needs custom work.
distractors.D: Raw curl calls give up typed tools, clear descriptions, and structured errors, and spread credentials across shell commands.

questions.hint: MCP integration vs build/reuse - reuse when safe, build when unique is needed.

questions.scenario: A developer asks Claude Code to find every place in a large repository that calls the function calculateTax, before changing its signature.
questions.question: Which kind of search fits this task?

options.text: A file-name pattern search for **/*tax*, then a review of the files it finds.
Reading every source file in the repository one by one, looking for the calls.
A content search for calculateTax across the files of the repository.
Asking the developer to list the files that use the function before starting.

explanation.correct: Finding callers means searching inside files for the function name, which is a content search (Grep, or grep through Bash, which Claude Code uses by default on macOS and Linux). A name-pattern search finds files by their names, not by what they contain.

distractors.A: Callers can live in files whose names have nothing to do with tax, so a name pattern misses them.
distractors.B: Reading every file wastes context and time when a content search finds the lines directly.
distractors.D: Claude can find the callers itself; asking the developer pushes back work the tools already do.

questions.hint: Use built-in tools with content search - search to find, built-in to execute.

questions.scenario: Before a test-framework migration, a developer asks Claude Code for a list of every test file in a repository. The files follow the naming convention *.spec.ts and are spread across many directories.
questions.question: Which kind of search fits this task?

options.text: A content search for the word describe( across all files in the repository.
Reading the src directory and checking each file name it contains by hand.
Listing only the top-level directory to see which test files are there.
A file-name pattern search such as **/*.spec.ts across the repository.

explanation.correct: Finding files by name is a name-pattern search (Glob, or find through Bash by default on macOS and Linux). A pattern like **/*.spec.ts matches at any depth.

distractors.A: describe( also appears in non-test code and misses spec files that do not use it, so it answers a different question.
distractors.B: Reading directories by hand is slow and misses files outside src.
distractors.C: A top-level listing misses the test files in nested directories.

questions.hint: File name search needs clear patterns - provide naming conventions to Claude.

questions.scenario: Claude Code tries to change a line return null; inside one function of a file. The Edit call fails because the text return null; appears three times in that file, and only one occurrence should change.
questions.question: What is the right next step?

options.text: Add lines from that function to old_string so it matches only once.
Rewrite the whole file with Write, reconstructing its contents from memory.
Set replace_all so that every occurrence of the text is changed at once.
Run a sed regular expression through Bash to change just the first match.

explanation.correct: Edit does exact string replacement and needs old_string to match exactly once. Adding enough surrounding context from the target function makes the match unique, so only that occurrence changes.

distractors.B: Rewriting a file from memory risks dropping or altering unrelated code. A full rewrite should start from a fresh Read, and it is unnecessary here.
distractors.C: replace_all changes all three occurrences, including the two that must stay.
distractors.D: The first match may not be the right one, and a shell substitution skips the exact-match check that makes Edit safe.

questions.hint: Edit tool with unique matching prevents race conditions - ensure right file editing.

questions.scenario: A new engineer asks Claude Code how checkout works in a 2,000-file repository. Claude starts reading every file under src/ in order, and its context fills with unrelated code before it reaches the checkout logic.
questions.question: What approach should Claude take instead?

options.text: Keep reading every file, since full coverage guarantees nothing important is missed.
Search for the checkout entry points, then read files by following their imports.
Read only the 20 largest files, since the core logic usually lives there.
List every file name with a pattern search, then read them in alphabetical order.

explanation.correct: Understanding builds best incrementally: a content search finds the entry points (routes, handlers, or a checkout function), then reading follows imports and calls outward. Context goes to the code that matters.

distractors.A: Reading everything uses up context on unrelated code, so the explanation suffers.
distractors.C: File size says little about relevance; checkout logic may live in small files.
distractors.D: Alphabetical order is as unrelated to checkout as the original approach.

questions.hint: Incremental exploration with progress indicators helps Claude learn interactively.

questions.scenario: Before removing a function called send, a developer asks Claude Code to find all of its callers. A content search for "send(" finds four. But the module utils/index.ts re-exports the function under other names, export { send as notifyUser, send as pushAlert }, and many modules import those names instead.
questions.question: How should Claude find every caller?

options.text: Broaden the search to the bare word send, without the parenthesis, across the repository.
Read every file that imports anything at all from the utils module.
List every name utils/index.ts exports for the function, then search for each name.
Search for files with notify in their names, since those are likely callers.

explanation.correct: Aliased re-exports hide callers from a search for the original name. Collecting every exported name for the function from the wrapper (send, notifyUser, pushAlert) and searching for each one finds all the call sites.

distractors.A: The bare word send matches countless unrelated uses and still misses calls through notifyUser and pushAlert.
distractors.B: Reading every importer of utils works eventually, but it is slow and context-heavy compared with targeted searches.
distractors.D: File names are unrelated to which functions a file calls, so this misses most callers.

questions.hint: Wrapper tracing helps debug when things go wrong - trace the execution flow.

questions.scenario: A team lead wrote the team's lint and naming conventions in their own ~/.claude/CLAUDE.md. Claude Code follows them in the lead's sessions, but a new developer who cloned the repository last week finds that Claude ignores them entirely.
questions.question: What should the team change?

options.text: Ask the new developer to copy the lead's ~/.claude/CLAUDE.md onto their own machine.
Move the conventions into the project's CLAUDE.md and commit it to the repository.
Put the conventions in a CLAUDE.local.md file at the root of the repository.
Tell Claude to remember the conventions, so they are saved in auto memory.

explanation.correct: User-level instructions in ~/.claude/CLAUDE.md apply only to that user. Team conventions belong in the project CLAUDE.md (./CLAUDE.md or ./.claude/CLAUDE.md), which is shared with everyone through version control.

distractors.A: Copying works for one person but drifts as soon as the lead edits their file, and it repeats for every new hire.
distractors.C: CLAUDE.local.md is for personal, project-specific notes and is meant to be gitignored, so teammates never get it.
distractors.D: Auto memory is notes Claude keeps for one user. It is not shared with teammates.

questions.hint: Rules apply by path - file extensions determine which configurations are active.

questions.scenario: A developer wants Claude Code to know their personal sandbox URL and test account for one project. These details apply only to them and only to this repository, and they must never be committed.
questions.question: Where should the developer put them?

options.text: In the project's CLAUDE.md, under a heading marked as personal notes.
In ~/.claude/CLAUDE.md, so they are kept outside the repository.
In a rule file at .claude/rules/sandbox.md inside the project.
In CLAUDE.local.md at the project root, listed in .gitignore.

explanation.correct: CLAUDE.local.md holds personal, project-specific instructions. It loads alongside the project CLAUDE.md, and once it is in .gitignore it never reaches the repository.

distractors.A: The project CLAUDE.md is committed and shared, so every teammate would get the private details.
distractors.B: User-level instructions load in every project, not just this one.
distractors.C: .claude/rules/ is part of the project configuration and is normally committed, so it would be shared too.

questions.hint: Only reviewed questions appear in production - check review_status before builds.

questions.scenario: In a monorepo, shared standards live in docs/standards/: api.md, testing.md, and frontend.md. The payments package needs only api.md and testing.md, and its maintainers want its CLAUDE.md to include exactly those, staying in sync as the standards change.
questions.question: What is the best way to do this?

options.text: Import the two files with @ paths, relative to the package's CLAUDE.md.
Paste every standards file into the root CLAUDE.md so all packages see them all.
Copy api.md and testing.md into the payments package and edit the copies there.
Move all three standards files into one skill that each package can invoke.

explanation.correct: CLAUDE.md can import files with @path/to/file. Relative paths resolve from the file that contains the import, imports can nest up to four levels, and the imported content stays in sync with its source.

distractors.B: Loading every standard into every package wastes context and gives payments the frontend rules it does not need.
distractors.C: Copies drift from the shared standards as soon as either one changes.
distractors.D: Standards that should always apply belong in always-loaded instructions. A skill loads only when it is invoked or judged relevant.

questions.hint: Path matching works correctly - ensure tool paths match actual file locations.

questions.scenario: The root CLAUDE.md says "Indent with 2 spaces." The legacy services/payments/CLAUDE.md says "Indent with 4 spaces." A developer starts Claude Code at the repository root and asks it to edit files in services/payments/, but the indentation Claude uses is inconsistent.
questions.question: What should the team do?

options.text: Nothing. A subdirectory CLAUDE.md fully replaces the root file for files in that folder.
Nothing. The root CLAUDE.md always takes priority, so 2 spaces will win in the end.
Scope the payments rule explicitly as an override for that directory.
Rename the payments file to CLAUDE.local.md so that Claude Code gives it a higher priority.

explanation.correct: CLAUDE.md files are concatenated, not overridden. The payments file loads once Claude works in that directory, so both rules sit in context and conflict. Making the payments rule explicit ("In services/payments/, indent with 4 spaces; this overrides the root rule") resolves the ambiguity.

distractors.A: Subdirectory files are added to context alongside the root file. They do not replace it.
distractors.B: There is no priority rule that makes the root file win. Both instructions are present and contradict each other.
distractors.D: CLAUDE.local.md is for personal, uncommitted notes. Renaming hides the rule from teammates and still leaves two conflicting instructions.

questions.hint: Terraform rules load for .tf files - path-scoped configs work by extension.

questions.scenario: Four teams edit one 600-line project CLAUDE.md covering testing, API conventions, deployment, and security. Every section applies to all work in the repository, but the file causes constant merge conflicts and is hard to navigate.
questions.question: How should the team reorganize it?

options.text: Keep one file, and add a table of contents at the top with links to each section.
Split it into topic files under .claude/rules/, such as testing.md and api.md.
Turn each section into a skill that Claude loads only when it judges one relevant.
Move each section into the CLAUDE.md files of the developers who maintain that area.

explanation.correct: .claude/rules/ holds topic-specific rule files. Rules without paths frontmatter load at launch, alongside the project CLAUDE.md, so behavior stays the same while each team owns a small file.

distractors.A: A table of contents helps navigation but leaves four teams editing one file, so the merge conflicts remain.
distractors.C: These rules apply to all work. Skills load on demand, so the rules would sometimes be missing.
distractors.D: Personal ~/.claude/CLAUDE.md files are not shared, so most of the team would lose the rules.

questions.hint: Gitignore excludes local notes - keep local configs out of version control.

questions.scenario: A team writes a /deploy-prod skill that runs their production release steps. They want it to run only when a developer types /deploy-prod, never because Claude decided on its own that it seemed relevant.
questions.question: How should the skill be configured?

options.text: Write "never run this automatically" at the start of the skill's description.
Set user-invocable: false in the skill's frontmatter.
Set disable-model-invocation: true in the skill's frontmatter.
Move the release steps into the project CLAUDE.md file instead.

explanation.correct: disable-model-invocation: true stops Claude from loading the skill by itself. Developers can still run it with /deploy-prod. Its description is not even placed in context until the skill is invoked.

distractors.A: A note in the description is guidance Claude may or may not follow. The frontmatter flag is the documented control.
distractors.B: user-invocable: false does the opposite: it hides the skill from the / menu so only Claude can invoke it.
distractors.D: CLAUDE.md is always loaded, so the release steps would sit in context all the time and could be acted on unasked.

questions.hint: Check PR reviews before merging - verify all content passes validation.

questions.scenario: A /audit-deps skill scans every package manifest and prints hundreds of lines of findings into the main conversation. Developers run it in the middle of feature work and then find that Claude has lost track of earlier decisions.
questions.question: What change helps most?

options.text: Add context: fork so the audit runs in a subagent; only its result returns.
Shorten the skill's instructions so that the skill itself takes up less context.
Tell developers to run /compact every time after they have used the skill.
Move the audit instructions into the project CLAUDE.md file instead.

explanation.correct: With context: fork, Claude Code runs the skill in a separate subagent context and returns its result, so the verbose output stays out of the main conversation.

distractors.B: The instructions are short. The bulk comes from the output the audit produces.
distractors.C: Compaction after the fact summarizes the noise along with the earlier decisions instead of keeping it out in the first place.
distractors.D: Moving the instructions to CLAUDE.md loads them in every session and still prints the output into the conversation.

questions.hint: /release command runs subagents properly - skills can launch independent work.

questions.scenario: A team adds context: fork to a /summarize-decisions skill that is meant to list the decisions made so far in the current conversation. Since the change, the skill returns generic advice that mentions none of the actual decisions.
questions.question: What is the cause, and the fix?

options.text: The forked subagent runs on a smaller model, so set a stronger model in the agent field.
The skill needs an agent field naming a subagent type, so add one for the fork to use.
The instructions are too short for a subagent, so expand them with more detail on format.
A forked skill can't see the conversation, so remove context: fork from this skill.

explanation.correct: A forked skill runs as a subagent that receives the skill content as its prompt and does not see the conversation history. A skill whose job is to read the current conversation must run in the main context.

distractors.A: Model choice is not the problem. No model can summarize a conversation it was never given.
distractors.B: The agent field picks which subagent type runs the fork, but every forked subagent lacks the conversation history.
distractors.C: More instructions cannot replace the missing conversation, which is what the skill needs.

questions.hint: Tests run locally - verify tool behavior matches documentation.

questions.scenario: A team has two kinds of guidance: coding standards that apply to every change in the repository, and a 14-step release checklist that is used about once a week.
questions.question: Where should each one live?

options.text: Both in the project CLAUDE.md, so that Claude always has all of the guidance in context.
Standards in the project CLAUDE.md, and the release checklist in a project skill.
Both as project skills, so Claude loads each one only when it seems relevant.
Standards in a project skill, and the release checklist in the project CLAUDE.md.

explanation.correct: CLAUDE.md is loaded in every session, which suits rules that apply to all work. A skill's body loads only when it is used, which suits an occasional multi-step procedure and keeps it from taking up context the rest of the week.

distractors.A: The checklist would cost context in every session for a task done weekly.
distractors.C: Standards that must always apply should not depend on Claude deciding they are relevant.
distractors.D: This swaps the two: always-needed rules would load on demand, and an occasional procedure would load all the time.

questions.hint: Review.sh validates JSON - structured scripts enable automation.

questions.scenario: A team's /fix-issue skill needs an issue number to work. Developers often type /fix-issue without one, and Claude then spends a turn asking which issue they meant.
questions.question: What frontmatter change helps developers supply the argument up front?

options.text: Rename the skill to /fix-issue-number so that the need is obvious.
Add a note about the required number to the project's CLAUDE.md.
Add argument-hint: [issue-number] to the frontmatter.
Have the skill tell Claude to pick the most recently opened issue.

explanation.correct: argument-hint shows the expected arguments in autocomplete as a developer types the command, so they see that an issue number is needed before sending.

distractors.A: A longer name hints at the need but is not a documented mechanism, and it makes the command harder to type.
distractors.B: CLAUDE.md is model context. It does not change what developers see while typing the command.
distractors.D: Guessing the issue risks working on the wrong one.

questions.hint: Checklist verifies setup - walk through each step methodically.

questions.scenario: A team adds allowed-tools: Read Grep to the frontmatter of a /review skill, expecting this to stop Claude from running shell commands during reviews. During a review, Claude still asks to run a Bash command, and a developer approves it.
questions.question: What explains this, and what would actually limit the tools?

options.text: It only pre-approves tools. Run the skill with context: fork, using an agent with a restricted tool list.
allowed-tools is ignored in project skills and only takes effect in personal skills.
The field name is misspelled. Skills read allowedTools in camelCase, not allowed-tools.
allowed-tools applies only in non-interactive -p runs, never in interactive sessions.

explanation.correct: Per current docs, allowed-tools lists tools Claude can use without asking during the turn that invokes the skill. It grants permission and does not remove other tools. To limit tools, run the skill with context: fork using an agent whose tools list is restricted, or add permission deny rules.

distractors.B: Nothing in the docs limits allowed-tools to personal skills. It works the same way in project skills.
distractors.C: allowed-tools is the documented frontmatter field name for skills.
distractors.D: The field applies in interactive sessions too. It just means "don't ask", not "only these".

questions.hint: CLAUDE.md rules apply everywhere - they define coding standards.

questions.scenario: A developer created a personal ~/.claude/skills/deploy skill that differs from the team's project .claude/skills/deploy skill. When they type /deploy, their own version runs, and their deployments no longer match what teammates get.
questions.question: What should the developer do?

options.text: Delete the team's project skill so that only one /deploy skill exists in total.
Rename the personal variant, so /deploy runs the team's version for everyone.
Move the personal variant into CLAUDE.local.md so that it stays out of git.
Add a priority: low field to the personal skill's frontmatter to rank it lower.

explanation.correct: When a personal skill and a project skill share a name, the personal one wins for that user. Giving the personal variant its own name, such as /deploy-sandbox, keeps it available without shadowing the team's /deploy.

distractors.A: Deleting the team's skill breaks /deploy for everyone else.
distractors.C: CLAUDE.local.md holds instructions, not invocable skills, so the variant would stop being a command.
distractors.D: There is no priority field for skills. Precedence is fixed by location.

questions.hint: Review status determines visibility - only reviewed content is deployed.

questions.scenario: Terraform conventions currently sit in the root CLAUDE.md and load in every session, even though most work never touches Terraform. The repository has Terraform files under infra/ and also in deploy/ folders inside many service directories.
questions.question: What is the best way to load these conventions only when they are needed?

options.text: Keep them in the root CLAUDE.md, under a clearly marked Terraform heading.
Put a copy of the conventions in a CLAUDE.md in every folder with .tf files.
Add a .claude/rules/ file with paths: ["**/*.tf"] frontmatter.
Turn the conventions into a skill that developers run before editing Terraform.

explanation.correct: A rule with paths frontmatter loads only when Claude works with matching files, wherever they are. One glob covers .tf files in infra/ and in every service's deploy/ folder.

distractors.A: A heading does not change loading. The conventions still cost context in every session.
distractors.B: Copies in many folders drift apart, and new deploy folders need yet another copy.
distractors.D: A manually run skill depends on developers remembering it, while the rule applies automatically.

questions.hint: Path-specific rules load conditionally - the paths frontmatter determines when a rule activates.

questions.scenario: A rule in .claude/rules/migrations.md has paths: ["db/migrations/**/*.sql"]. A developer asks Claude a general question about the team's migration strategy, without referring to any migration file, and the answer ignores the rule.
questions.question: What explains this?

options.text: Path-scoped rules load only once Claude works with a matching file.
Rules load only at session start, so the developer must restart Claude Code first.
Rules apply only after being imported into CLAUDE.md with an @ path reference.
Rule files in .claude/rules/ are only read while the session is in plan mode.

explanation.correct: A rule with paths is conditional: it loads when Claude works with files matching its patterns. A question that touches no migration file never triggers it. Referencing a migration file loads it, and if the rule should always apply, remove its paths field.

distractors.B: Unscoped rules load at launch, but path-scoped rules load on demand, so a restart would not help.
distractors.C: Rules in .claude/rules/ are discovered automatically and need no import.
distractors.D: Rules are not tied to plan mode.

questions.hint: Conditional rules activate based on file types - if no matching file, the rule never loads.

questions.scenario: A rule file starts with the frontmatter paths: [**/*.tsx], written without quotes. The team expected its React conventions to apply only to .tsx files, but the rule now appears in context in every session, even for backend-only work.
questions.question: What is the most likely cause?

options.text: Claude Code ignores paths in project rules and only reads it in user-level rules.
Rule files must sit directly in .claude/rules/, not inside a subdirectory of it.
Rule files with frontmatter must use a .yaml extension instead of a .md one.
The YAML failed to parse, so the rule loaded unscoped. Quote the patterns.

explanation.correct: In YAML an unquoted * starts an alias, so this frontmatter does not parse. When frontmatter fails to parse, Claude Code ignores it and loads the rule as if it had no paths. Quoting the patterns (paths: ["**/*.tsx"]) fixes it, and claude --debug shows the parse error.

distractors.A: paths works in project rules. That is its main use.
distractors.B: Rule files are discovered recursively, so subdirectories such as frontend/ are fine.
distractors.C: Rules are Markdown files with YAML frontmatter. The .md extension is correct.

questions.hint: YAML frontmatter must parse correctly - unquoted strings starting with * cause parse failures that are silently ignored.

questions.scenario: A developer has a failing test with a clear stack trace that points to a missing null check in one function of one file. The fix is obvious and touches about three lines.
questions.question: How should they approach this with Claude Code?

options.text: Enter plan mode and have Claude produce a plan before it changes anything.
Have a subagent map the whole repository first to understand the context.
Use direct execution: ask Claude to add the null check and rerun the test.
Write a short design document first, then ask Claude to implement it.

explanation.correct: Direct execution suits small, well-understood changes with a clear scope. Here the cause is known and the change is local, so planning adds time without reducing risk.

distractors.A: Plan mode pays off for large or ambiguous changes. For a three-line fix with a clear stack trace it only adds a step.
distractors.B: Mapping the repository wastes time and context on a problem the stack trace already pinpoints.
distractors.D: A design document is far more process than a known three-line fix needs.

questions.scenario: A team must replace a deprecated date library used in about 60 files. Some call sites could switch to native date APIs, others need a small adapter, and nobody knows yet how the usages split between the two.
questions.question: How should they use Claude Code?

options.text: Plan mode to inventory usages and pick an approach, then execute the plan.
Ask Claude to convert all 60 files in one direct pass and fix failing tests afterwards.
Have four developers each convert 15 files in separate sessions, starting right away.
Convert only the files touched this sprint and leave the rest for some later sprint.

explanation.correct: This change spans many files and has more than one valid approach, so exploring first pays off. In plan mode Claude reads the code and proposes a plan without editing. Once the plan is approved, executing it directly is efficient.

distractors.B: Converting without knowing which approach fits each call site risks rework across 60 files.
distractors.C: Parallel sessions without a shared plan will choose different approaches for similar call sites.
distractors.D: Leaving the migration half done keeps both libraries in the codebase indefinitely.
