questions.hint: Plan mode explores alternatives for large changes - use it when many files are affected or multiple approaches exist.

questions.scenario: During a multi-phase refactor, Claude's discovery phase (hundreds of search results and many file reads) fills most of the main conversation's context before any implementation begins.
questions.question: What should the developer do in the next refactor?

options.text: Run /clear after discovery so that implementation starts with an empty context.
Switch to a model with a larger context window for the discovery phase.
Save the search results to a file and have Claude read that file back later.
Delegate discovery to a subagent that explores and returns only a summary.

explanation.correct: A subagent explores in its own context window and returns only its findings, so the main conversation keeps room for implementation. Claude Code's built-in Explore agent exists for this kind of read-only discovery.

distractors.A: Clearing discards the findings along with the noise, so implementation starts without what discovery learned.
distractors.B: A bigger window postpones the problem and still fills the main context with raw search output.
distractors.C: Reading the saved file back puts the same volume of output into the main context.

questions.hint: Exploration subagents run in isolation - they discover context without consuming the main conversation window.

questions.scenario: A team now runs every change through plan mode, including typo fixes and one-line config edits, and velocity has dropped. A senior engineer proposes dropping plan mode entirely and relying on code review instead.
questions.question: Which policy fits best?

options.text: Keep plan mode for every change, since a plan never makes a change any less safe.
Plan for multi-file or multi-approach changes; go direct otherwise.
Drop plan mode entirely and rely on code review to catch the design problems instead.
Use plan mode only when a change will touch more than three files in the repository.

explanation.correct: Plan mode is for changes with architectural impact, several valid approaches, or many files. Small, clear changes are faster with direct execution. Deciding by those properties keeps the safety where it matters without slowing everything.

distractors.A: Planning trivial edits costs time with no benefit, which is the slowdown the team already has.
distractors.C: Code review catches problems after the work is done, when a wrong approach is expensive to undo.
distractors.D: File count is a crude proxy. A one-file change can need design work, and a mechanical change can touch many files.

questions.hint: Plan mode handles architectural changes - skip it for small, well-defined edits with clear scope.

questions.scenario: An engineer wants Claude Code to analyze a repository of production configuration and propose changes. Nothing may be modified until a second engineer has reviewed the proposal.
questions.question: What is the best way to run the session?

options.text: Use direct execution and put "do not edit any files" at the start of the prompt.
Use direct execution and rely on git to revert any edits Claude makes by mistake.
Use plan mode: Claude reads and proposes, but edits nothing until approved.
Make every file read-only on disk, then use direct execution as normal.

explanation.correct: In plan mode Claude reads files and proposes a plan but makes no edits until the plan is approved. You enter it with Shift+Tab or claude --permission-mode plan. That matches "analyze and propose, change nothing yet".

distractors.A: A prompt instruction is guidance, not a guarantee.
distractors.B: Reverting after the fact still allows unreviewed changes to land first.
distractors.D: Changing file permissions is a heavy workaround for what plan mode provides directly, and it is easy to forget to undo.

questions.hint: Plan mode separates proposal from action - enter it to design, then approve before editing.

questions.scenario: A developer describes in prose how legacy address strings should be normalized. Each time Claude implements it, the result differs in small ways, such as abbreviations and the order of the parts.
questions.question: What is the most effective next step?

options.text: Rewrite the prose description so that it is longer and much more detailed.
Give two or three concrete input and expected-output examples.
Ask Claude to take extra care and to double-check its work every time.
Switch to a different model that may read the prose more consistently.

explanation.correct: When prose is read inconsistently, a few concrete input/output pairs remove the ambiguity. They show exactly how to handle abbreviations and ordering.

distractors.A: More prose usually adds more ways to interpret it.
distractors.C: "Take care" adds no information about what the right output is.
distractors.D: The ambiguity lives in the specification, not the model.

questions.hint: Input/output examples clarify ambiguity - concrete examples remove uncertainty in handling edge cases.

questions.scenario: A team needs a rate limiter with tricky edge cases: bursts at window boundaries, clock skew, and a requirement to handle 10,000 checks per second. Earlier attempts looked right in review but failed in production.
questions.question: Which workflow fits best?

options.text: Have Claude write the limiter, then ask Claude whether it handles all the edge cases.
Describe the edge cases in prose, then review the code Claude writes line by line.
Have Claude write the limiter and its tests together, and trust that the tests pass.
Write tests for behavior, edge cases, and throughput first; iterate on failures.

explanation.correct: Tests written first define the behavior, edge cases, and performance requirement objectively. Claude then iterates against real failures, which you share back each round, instead of against a reading of prose.

distractors.A: Asking whether the code is right gets an opinion, not evidence.
distractors.B: Line-by-line review is how the earlier attempts slipped through.
distractors.C: Tests written alongside the code tend to share its blind spots.

questions.hint: Test-driven iteration uses real failures - write tests first to define behavior, then fix against actual failures.

questions.scenario: A developer has to add a caching layer to a pricing service but has never designed caches before. They worry about missing something important, such as how prices are invalidated, or what happens when the cache is down.
questions.question: How should they start the session with Claude?

options.text: Ask Claude to interview them about requirements before coding.
Ask Claude to implement a cache right away, then fix the problems as they show up.
Paste in a generic caching tutorial and ask Claude to follow it step by step.
Tell Claude to be thorough and to think of everything while it implements.

explanation.correct: Having Claude ask questions first (the interview pattern) surfaces considerations the developer did not know to mention, such as invalidation rules, staleness limits, and failure modes, before any code exists.

distractors.B: In an unfamiliar domain, fixing problems as they appear means discovering design flaws late.
distractors.C: A generic tutorial cannot cover this service's pricing and invalidation needs.
distractors.D: "Think of everything" does not reveal what the developer actually needs.

questions.hint: The interview pattern surfaces needs - ask questions first to discover requirements the developer didn't document.

questions.scenario: Reviewing a data-migration script, a developer finds three problems. Null dates crash the parser. The date-format fix changes which rows reach the null-handling path. And there is an unrelated typo in a log message.
questions.question: How should they give Claude the feedback?

options.text: Send one issue per message, in the order they were found, whatever the dependency.
Collect every comment on the whole repository and send all of them in one message.
Send the two linked problems together; send the typo separately.
Fix the two linked problems by hand and ask Claude only to correct the log typo.

explanation.correct: Issues that interact should be described together, so Claude can design one consistent fix. Independent issues can be handled separately. The null and date problems interact; the typo does not.

distractors.A: Fixing the date format alone changes the null path. One at a time invites back-and-forth and rework.
distractors.B: Unrelated comments from across the repository dilute the message and blur which problems interact.
distractors.D: Doing the hard part by hand gives up Claude's help where it is most useful.

questions.hint: Interacting issues need unified description - describe related problems together for consistent solutions.

questions.scenario: A CI job runs Claude Code on each pull request and posts findings as inline comments. The script currently asks Claude to "respond in JSON" and parses the text, which breaks whenever Claude adds a sentence before the JSON.
questions.question: What is the most reliable fix?

options.text: Add "respond with only JSON and nothing else" to the prompt in capital letters.
Use --output-format stream-json and extract the JSON with a regular expression.
Run the job with --verbose so the output contains complete debugging details.
Use --output-format json with --json-schema; read structured_output.

explanation.correct: With --output-format json and --json-schema, the response carries schema-conforming data in structured_output, separate from any prose. The script should check the field exists, because a run that ends without valid output leaves it out.

distractors.A: Stronger wording makes clean JSON more likely, but parsing still breaks on the occasional extra sentence.
distractors.B: stream-json gives event lines, not schema-validated findings, so the regular expression stays fragile.
distractors.C: --verbose adds detail to the output. It does not structure the findings.

questions.hint: CI structured output uses JSON schema - --output-format json with --json-schema enables programmatic result handling.

questions.scenario: A CI review job runs again on every new commit to a pull request. Each run reposts comments the previous run already made about issues the author has not fixed yet, so pull requests fill up with duplicate comments.
questions.question: What change addresses this best?

options.text: Pass the previous findings; ask for only new or still-open issues.
Delete all earlier review comments before every run and repost them from scratch.
Run the review only on the first commit of each pull request and never again.
Drop new comments whose text exactly matches a comment that was posted before.

explanation.correct: Giving Claude the prior findings lets it report only new issues and ones that remain open, which keeps the thread readable and still catches regressions.

distractors.B: Deleting and reposting erases the discussion history on each comment.
distractors.C: Reviewing only the first commit misses problems introduced later.
distractors.D: Claude rarely words a finding the same way twice, so exact-text matching misses most duplicates.

questions.hint: Review iterations avoid duplicate findings - give prior findings so Claude reports only new or remaining issues.

questions.scenario: A team has Claude Code generate a feature and then, in the same session, asks it to review its own changes. The reviews rarely find problems, yet human reviewers keep catching subtle bugs afterwards.
questions.question: What change would most improve the reviews?

options.text: Ask the same session to review its code a second time, much more carefully.
Turn on more reasoning effort for the review step within the same session.
Review in a separate, fresh Claude instance that didn't write the code.
Ask the session to list any doubts it had while it was writing the code.

explanation.correct: A session that wrote the code carries its own reasoning and assumptions, which makes it less likely to question them. An independent instance without that context reviews the change as written.

distractors.A: A second pass in the same session repeats the same blind spots.
distractors.B: More effort within the same context still reasons from the same assumptions.
distractors.D: Self-reported doubts show what the session noticed, not what it missed.

questions.hint: Independent reviews catch assumptions - a fresh session without code context questions the reasoning behind the code.

questions.scenario: Following the docs' advice for CI, a team runs claude --bare -p for automated test generation. The generated tests ignore the fixture and naming conventions written in the project's CLAUDE.md, although the same prompt follows them in interactive sessions.
questions.question: What explains this, and what is the fix?

options.text: CLAUDE.md never loads in -p mode, so the team must stop running Claude Code in CI.
--bare skips CLAUDE.md, so pass the conventions with --append-system-prompt-file.
CI runners cannot read dotfiles, so the CLAUDE.md file must be renamed for CI.
Test generation ignores project context, so add the conventions to every test prompt.

explanation.correct: Bare mode skips auto-discovery of hooks, skills, MCP servers, auto memory, and CLAUDE.md, so CI runs are reproducible across machines. Context has to be passed explicitly, for example with --append-system-prompt-file pointing at the conventions. Without --bare, -p loads CLAUDE.md as usual.

distractors.A: -p loads CLAUDE.md normally. It is --bare that skips it.
distractors.C: CLAUDE.md is not a dotfile, and the runner can read it. Bare mode chooses not to.
distractors.D: Pasting the conventions into every prompt works but duplicates them. The documented route is a system prompt file.

questions.hint: Bare mode ensures reproducibility - it skips auto-discovery for consistent CI runs across environments.

questions.scenario: A nightly job runs claude -p "Run the test suite and fix any failures". Logs show Claude tried to run npm test several times, but each call was denied, and the job ended without running a single test.
questions.question: What should the team change?

options.text: Pre-approve the test command with --allowedTools "Bash(npm test *)".
Add a line to CLAUDE.md saying Claude may run the test suite in CI.
Run the job interactively so someone can approve each command it needs.
Use --permission-mode bypassPermissions so that nothing ever asks.

explanation.correct: In a -p run, calls that need approval are denied unless something approves them. --allowedTools with permission rule syntax pre-approves exactly the commands the job needs, here npm test with any arguments.

distractors.B: CLAUDE.md is instructions, not permissions, so the calls would still be denied.
distractors.C: A nightly job has nobody to approve commands.
distractors.D: Bypassing every permission is far broader than the job needs, and the docs reserve it for isolated environments.

questions.hint: Permissions control tool approval - --allowedTools pre-approves specific tools for non-interactive CI runs.

questions.scenario: A nightly CI job asks Claude Code to add tests for recently changed modules. Developers find that many generated tests duplicate scenarios the existing suite already covers, and others ignore the team's shared fixtures.
questions.question: What change most improves the generated tests?

options.text: Ask Claude to generate twice as many tests so that more of them end up being new.
Delete generated tests whose names match existing ones after every nightly run.
Switch the job to a different model for test generation only, keeping the prompt.
Give it the existing tests; document fixtures and standards in CLAUDE.md.

explanation.correct: Claude can only avoid duplicates it can see, so the existing tests for each module belong in context. Documenting the testing standards and available fixtures in CLAUDE.md (or passing them explicitly when running with --bare) steers new tests toward real gaps and the team's conventions.

distractors.A: More tests produce more duplicates, and more noise for reviewers.
distractors.B: Matching names misses duplicates with different names, and does nothing about the ignored fixtures.
distractors.C: The problem is missing context, not the model.

questions.hint: CI test generation needs existing context - include current tests so Claude can avoid duplicating coverage.

questions.scenario: A support-triage assistant is told "Mark tickets as urgent when they are important." It marks about 40% of tickets urgent, including password-reset requests, and agents have started ignoring the label.
questions.question: What change most improves the precision of the urgent label?

options.text: Tell the assistant to mark a ticket urgent only when it is very confident.
Tell the assistant to be much more conservative with the urgent label.
Define urgent: a multi-user outage, data loss, or a security incident.
Add a reminder at the end of the prompt that urgent means truly important.

explanation.correct: Explicit, categorical criteria tell Claude exactly which tickets qualify. Vague words such as "important" or "conservative" leave the boundary to interpretation, so precision barely moves.

distractors.A: Confidence wording does not define what counts as urgent, so the same tickets keep qualifying.
distractors.B: "Be conservative" is a general instruction that fails to improve precision compared with specific criteria.
distractors.D: Restating "important" repeats the same vague criterion that caused the problem.

questions.hint: Validate invoices by checking data types and required fields first.

questions.scenario: A code-scanning assistant reports eight categories of issues. Logs show its "unused variable" category is wrong about 70% of the time, while its injection and authentication findings are almost always right. Developers have started dismissing every finding without reading it.
questions.question: What should the team do first?

options.text: Pause the noisy category while fixing its prompt; keep the accurate ones.
Keep all eight categories and add "only report findings you are sure about".
Turn off the assistant entirely until every category reaches high precision.
Show a model-reported confidence score next to every finding in the report.

explanation.correct: A high false-positive category undermines trust in the accurate ones. Temporarily disabling it restores trust in the injection and authentication findings while its criteria are rewritten.

distractors.B: A general "be sure" instruction does not fix vague criteria, and the noisy category keeps eroding trust meanwhile.
distractors.C: Switching everything off throws away the accurate security findings developers need.
distractors.D: An uncalibrated confidence score adds a number without removing the noise developers are reacting to.

questions.scenario: A review assistant labels findings as high, medium, or low severity. The same kind of issue, such as a missing input check on an internal endpoint, is rated high one day and low the next, which makes the severity column useless for triage.
questions.question: What change best makes the severity ratings consistent?

options.text: Ask the assistant to be consistent with its earlier ratings in each review.
Run every finding through the assistant twice and keep the lower rating.
Let developers override the severity rating whenever they disagree with it.
Define each severity level explicitly, with concrete code examples of each.

explanation.correct: Explicit severity definitions, each illustrated with concrete code examples, give Claude a fixed reference point, so the same pattern gets the same rating.

distractors.A: Without stable definitions, there is nothing for "consistent" to anchor to.
distractors.B: Running twice and keeping the lower rating biases results downward without defining the levels.
distractors.C: Manual overrides fix individual cases after the fact but leave the ratings inconsistent.

questions.scenario: A notification service sends Claude-written messages as SMS. The system prompt says "NEVER use markdown." Messages still sometimes contain asterisks and pound signs, and occasionally numbered lists that look broken on phones.
questions.question: Which prompt change is most likely to fix this?

options.text: Repeat "NEVER use markdown" three times, in capital letters, in the prompt.
Explain that replies go out as SMS, which shows markup symbols as raw text.
List every markdown symbol that must not appear anywhere in the replies.
Remove the instruction and rely on the phone to strip any formatting symbols.

explanation.correct: Giving the reason behind an instruction helps Claude generalize. Knowing the output is plain-text SMS, it avoids every kind of formatting that would look broken, including cases a symbol list would miss.

distractors.A: Emphasis alone does not tell Claude why, so edge cases such as numbered lists persist.
distractors.C: A symbol list covers only what you thought of, while the reason covers the whole category.
distractors.D: Phones show markdown as raw characters. Nothing strips it.

questions.hint: Pair tool results by custom_id - matching is essential for accuracy.

questions.scenario: A pull-request reviewer prompt already says "Only report high-confidence findings," yet precision has not improved. An engineer proposes adding "Be extremely conservative" and filtering out findings whose self-reported confidence is below 0.8.
questions.question: What is the most effective change?

options.text: Add "be extremely conservative" on top of the existing high-confidence instruction.
Filter out findings below 0.8 on the model's self-reported confidence score.
Name the categories to report (bugs, security) and to skip (style).
Add few-shot examples that show only findings the model was highly confident in.

explanation.correct: General caution instructions do not improve precision as well as specific categorical criteria. Defining what to report and what to skip removes whole classes of noise at the source.

distractors.A: Stacking more caution wording is the same approach that already failed.
distractors.B: Confidence filtering sounds rigorous, but uncalibrated self-reported confidence is a weak signal, and it leaves the criteria vague.
distractors.D: Examples of confident findings do not tell Claude which categories are out of scope.

questions.hint: Batch processing needs ordered lists - maintain sequence guarantees.

questions.scenario: A release-notes generator receives detailed formatting instructions. Even so, its bullets vary: some start with a verb and some with the component name, and some include ticket numbers while others do not.
questions.question: What is the most effective way to make the format consistent?

options.text: Add a few correctly formatted examples in <example> tags.
Make the format description longer, covering every possible variation.
Ask Claude to be more consistent with the format of its bullet points.
Put the most important formatting rules in bold within the instructions.

explanation.correct: Few-shot examples are one of the most reliable ways to steer format and structure when instructions alone produce inconsistent results. Wrapping them in tags separates them from the instructions.

distractors.B: More description leaves more room for interpretation, which is the problem.
distractors.C: Asking for consistency gives Claude nothing concrete to be consistent with.
distractors.D: Bold text adds emphasis, not a concrete target format.

questions.hint: Error categories help handle different failure modes appropriately.

questions.scenario: A bug-summary prompt includes four examples, all about payment-processing bugs. Summaries of unrelated bugs, such as a broken image upload, now often mention payments or use payment terminology.
questions.question: How should the team fix the examples?

options.text: Remove the examples and go back to instructions only.
Add ten more payment examples to strengthen the pattern.
Note that the examples are illustrative and not literal.
Use varied examples across areas, including edge cases.

explanation.correct: Examples should be relevant and diverse. Four examples from one domain teach an unintended pattern, so varying them across areas and edge cases teaches the format without the payment bias.

distractors.A: Dropping the examples loses their benefit for format and consistency.
distractors.B: More of the same examples strengthens the unwanted payment bias.
distractors.C: A disclaimer is weak compared with the pattern the examples themselves set.

questions.hint: Tool execution errors need proper categorization and handling.

questions.scenario: A support-routing agent handles clear requests well but is inconsistent on ambiguous ones, such as "I want a refund for a gift I received", which could go to returns or to billing depending on details.
questions.question: What change best improves its handling of ambiguous requests?

options.text: Write every routing rule out in prose, and add more rules for the edge cases.
Add ambiguous examples that explain why one route beat the other.
Give the agent more routing tools so each ambiguous case has its own option.
Send every request that looks ambiguous straight to a human agent instead.

explanation.correct: Few-shot examples that show the reasoning for ambiguous cases (why returns rather than billing, given the details) let Claude generalize that judgment to new ambiguous requests.

distractors.A: More prose rules rarely cover the next ambiguous case and tend to conflict with each other.
distractors.C: More tools add choices without teaching the judgment.
distractors.D: Escalating every ambiguous request sends routine work to humans.

questions.hint: Message structure must be correct for tool_use blocks.

questions.scenario: A recipe-extraction pipeline fills a numeric quantity field. Sources often use informal amounts such as "a pinch", "a couple of cups", or "a splash", and Claude invents precise numbers for them, such as 0.31 cups.
questions.question: What change best reduces the invented values?

options.text: Tell Claude to be precise when it extracts quantities from recipes.
Make the numeric quantity field required for every ingredient.
Add examples that keep informal amounts as text with quantity null.
Replace the extraction with regular expressions over the recipe text.

explanation.correct: Few-shot examples that show informal amounts handled correctly (the original phrase kept as text and the numeric field left empty) reduce made-up precision and generalize to phrasings the examples do not list.

distractors.A: "Be precise" pushes toward exact numbers, which is the fabrication being fixed.
distractors.B: A required numeric field forces Claude to produce a number even when none exists.
distractors.D: Regular expressions cannot handle the variety of informal phrasings.

questions.hint: Send tools need all required parameters - validate upfront.

questions.scenario: A research pipeline extracts citations from papers. It works on papers with inline citations but misses most citations in papers that use a bibliography section with numbered references. An engineer proposes classifying each paper's format first and maintaining a separate prompt for each format.
questions.question: What is the most effective first change?

options.text: Add examples of both inline citations and numbered bibliographies.
Build the format classifier and keep a separate prompt for each format.
Tell Claude that citations can appear anywhere in a paper.
Raise max_tokens so Claude has room to list more citations.

explanation.correct: Few-shot examples that show correct extraction from both structures teach Claude to handle structural variety in one prompt, which is the cheapest and most general fix.

distractors.B: A classifier with per-format prompts can work, but it adds a component to maintain and a new failure point, and every new format needs another prompt.
distractors.C: A general hint does not show how numbered references map to the text.
distractors.D: The extraction is not running out of space. It does not recognize the bibliography format.

questions.hint: Agent results need proper formatting - match expected schema.

questions.scenario: An extraction service asks Claude to "respond only with JSON" and parses the reply. About 2% of replies fail to parse, because of a trailing comment or a missing brace.
questions.question: What is the most reliable fix?

options.text: Repeat the "respond only with JSON" instruction more strongly.
Use structured outputs: a JSON schema in output_config.format.
Extract the text between the first and last brace before parsing.
Retry any reply that fails to parse until a valid one comes back.

explanation.correct: Structured outputs use constrained decoding to keep the response valid against the schema, which eliminates JSON syntax errors.

distractors.A: Stronger wording lowers the error rate but cannot guarantee valid JSON.
distractors.C: Trimming to the braces still fails when the JSON inside is malformed.
distractors.D: Retries cost extra calls and still have no guarantee of success.

questions.hint: ValidationError catches schema issues early - fail fast.

questions.scenario: An invoice extractor uses structured outputs with a strict schema, so every response is valid JSON with the right fields. Audits still find invoices where the line items do not add up to the extracted total.
questions.question: What should the team add?

options.text: Switch from JSON outputs to strict tool use, which validates inputs more strictly.
Add minimum and maximum constraints on the amounts in the JSON schema.
Add a prompt line insisting that all of the extracted amounts must add up.
Check the sums in code, and flag or retry the invoices that do not add up.

explanation.correct: Structured outputs guarantee the shape, not semantic correctness. Checking that line items add up has to happen in code, which can then retry with the specific error or send the invoice for review.

distractors.A: Strict tool use also guarantees shape, not arithmetic.
distractors.B: Numeric constraints such as minimum and maximum are not supported in structured-output schemas and return a 400, and they could not express "these add up" anyway.
distractors.C: A prompt line helps a little but guarantees nothing, and the audit gap remains.

questions.hint: Message coordination needs state tracking - track what was sent.

questions.scenario: A purchase-order extractor's schema makes po_number a required string. Many scanned documents have no PO number at all, and for those, Claude produces plausible-looking but invented numbers.
questions.question: What is the best fix?

options.text: Make po_number nullable, and tell Claude to use null when it is absent.
Keep po_number required and add a prompt line: "do not invent values".
Keep it required and tell Claude to write "N/A" whenever it is missing.
Remove po_number from the extraction, since it is too unreliable to keep.

explanation.correct: A required field forces a value even when the source has none, which invites fabrication. Making the field nullable, with an explicit rule to use null when the information is absent, lets the output be honest.

distractors.B: The schema still demands a value, so the instruction and the schema pull in opposite directions.
distractors.C: A sentinel string mixes "missing" into a real value field and breaks downstream type checks.
distractors.D: Removing the field loses the PO numbers that do exist.

questions.hint: Tool result validation prevents downstream errors - check early.

questions.scenario: A document classifier uses an enum category of invoice, receipt, or contract. Bank statements and tax forms, which fit none of these, are being classified as invoices.
questions.question: How should the schema change?

options.text: Expand the enum to list every document type the team can think of.
Replace the enum with a free-text category field filled by the model.
Add "other" with a detail field, and "unclear" for ambiguous documents.
Drop the category and let downstream systems work out the document type.

explanation.correct: An "other" value plus a detail string gives documents outside the list somewhere honest to go, and "unclear" handles genuinely ambiguous inputs. The known categories stay clean enums.

distractors.A: A huge enum is never complete, and the next unexpected type gets forced into the nearest bucket.
distractors.B: Free text loses the consistent labels downstream systems rely on.
distractors.D: Dropping the category pushes the problem downstream instead of solving it.

questions.hint: Extraction loops need retry on transient issues - be resilient.

questions.scenario: A travel assistant chats with users and calls a book_flight tool. About one call in fifty has a missing required field or a malformed date, and the booking API rejects it. An engineer proposes putting a JSON schema on output_config.format so every response is validated.
questions.question: What is the better fix?

options.text: Do it: put a JSON schema on output_config.format for every response.
Set strict: true on book_flight so its inputs always match its schema.
Tell Claude in the system prompt to always include every booking field.
Ask the user to confirm and re-enter each field whenever a call fails.

explanation.correct: Strict tool use guarantees that tool inputs match the tool's schema, which is exactly where the errors occur. JSON outputs (output_config.format) shape Claude's whole response, which would break the conversational replies.

distractors.A: Forcing the entire response into one JSON schema suits pure extraction, not an assistant that also chats.
distractors.C: A prompt rule lowers the error rate but cannot guarantee valid tool inputs.
distractors.D: Pushing validation onto the user adds friction for a problem the schema can prevent.

questions.hint: Pairing requires consistent IDs across requests and responses.

questions.scenario: A pipeline parses every structured-output response straight into its database. A few times a week it crashes on output that does not match the schema. Logs show those responses ended with stop_reason "max_tokens" on very long documents.
questions.question: What should the pipeline do?

options.text: Check stop_reason first; retry max_tokens cases with a higher limit.
Wrap the parsing in a try/catch block and skip any document that fails.
Remove the schema, since structured outputs evidently are not reliable.
Lower max_tokens so that the responses are shorter and finish in time.

explanation.correct: Structured outputs can fail to match the schema when the response is cut off by max_tokens, or when Claude refuses. Checking stop_reason before parsing, and retrying truncated responses with a higher max_tokens, handles both safely.

distractors.B: Skipping documents silently loses data.
distractors.C: The schema works. The cut-off responses are a separate, documented case to handle.
distractors.D: A lower limit makes truncation more frequent, not less.

questions.hint: JSON extraction handles partial data - be flexible but safe.

questions.scenario: An extraction fails validation because the total field is missing, even though the document clearly shows a total on page 2. The pipeline retries by sending the identical request again, and gets the same result.
questions.question: How should the retry be built?

options.text: Resend the identical request a few more times until it eventually passes.
Resend the request with "try again and be careful" added to the prompt.
Resend the request to a different model each time until one passes.
Send the document, the failed extraction, and the specific error back.

explanation.correct: Retry with error feedback works because Claude sees the original document, its previous answer, and exactly what failed ("total is missing; the document shows one on page 2"), so it can correct the specific problem.

distractors.A: An identical request tends to reproduce the identical mistake.
distractors.B: "Be careful" gives no information about what went wrong.
distractors.C: Switching models adds cost and still gives no feedback about the error.

questions.hint: Tool error propagation needs proper categorization.

questions.scenario: A contract pipeline retries five times whenever the contract end date is missing. For one vendor, every retry fails: the end date is defined only in a separate amendment that is never sent to Claude.
questions.question: What should the pipeline do?

options.text: Raise the retry limit to ten so the extraction has more chances to succeed.
Stop retrying, return null, and flag that the amendment is needed.
Tell Claude to infer a likely end date from the contract's other terms.
Switch to a larger model for documents that still fail after five retries.

explanation.correct: Retries fix format and structural errors, but they cannot produce information that is not in the input. When the data lives in a document that was not provided, the right result is an honest null plus a flag saying what is missing.

distractors.A: More retries cost more and still cannot find information that is not there.
distractors.C: Inferring the date creates a fabricated value in a contract system.
distractors.D: No model can read an amendment it was never given.

questions.hint: Message flow requires clear state tracking - avoid confusion.

questions.scenario: Developers dismiss about a third of an automated reviewer's findings. The team wants to reduce false positives but cannot tell which kinds of code produce the dismissed findings.
questions.question: What change helps most?

options.text: Add a detected_pattern field to each finding, and analyze dismissals by pattern.
Ask developers to write a free-text explanation every time they dismiss a finding.
Cap the reviewer at five findings per pull request to reduce the overall noise.
Add a confidence score to each finding and hide the low-confidence findings.

explanation.correct: Recording which code construct triggered each finding turns dismissals into data: the team can see which patterns are dismissed most and fix the criteria or examples for exactly those.

distractors.B: Free-text notes are slow to write and hard to aggregate across many reviews.
distractors.C: A cap hides findings, true and false alike, without showing what causes the noise.
distractors.D: Uncalibrated confidence scores do not reveal which patterns go wrong.

questions.hint: Batch tool calls to reduce round trips - be efficient.

questions.scenario: Some supplier invoices contain arithmetic errors in the source: the printed total does not equal the sum of the line items. The finance team wants these flagged, not silently corrected and not dropped.
questions.question: How should the extraction schema handle this?

options.text: Ask Claude to correct the total so that it always matches the line items.
Extract only the printed total and trust it, since it is what the supplier billed.
Extract the printed total and a calculated total, plus a conflict_detected flag.
Discard any invoice whose numbers do not add up, and log it for later.

explanation.correct: Capturing both the stated and the calculated totals, with a boolean flag for disagreement, preserves what the document says and exposes the conflict for review.

distractors.A: Silent correction hides a real billing discrepancy the finance team needs to see.
distractors.B: Trusting only the printed total misses the error entirely.
distractors.D: Discarding loses legitimate invoices that just need review.

questions.hint: Validate each tool result before next step - prevent cascading errors.

questions.scenario: Two extraction failures come back from validation. In the first, a date is written "3rd of May 2026" but the schema requires ISO 8601. In the second, the supplier's tax ID is empty, and the document contains no tax ID anywhere.
questions.question: How should the pipeline handle them?

options.text: Retry both with the original request until each extraction passes validation.
Retry neither, and send both straight to human review without any retry.
Retry the tax ID with feedback, and accept the date in its original format.
Retry the date with feedback; record the tax ID as missing in the source.

explanation.correct: Format errors respond well to retry-with-feedback, because the information is there and only its form is wrong. An absent value cannot be produced by retrying; it should be recorded as missing.

distractors.A: Retrying the tax ID wastes calls, or invites a made-up value.
distractors.B: Sending a fixable format error to humans spends reviewer time a retry would save.
distractors.C: This reverses the two: the date is fixable and the tax ID is not.

questions.hint: Structured error handling prevents data loss - validate before commit.

questions.scenario: Every Sunday night, a team classifies about 40,000 support tickets for a Monday-morning report. Nobody waits on individual results, and the team wants to cut the cost.
questions.question: Which approach fits best?

options.text: Keep the synchronous API, but run many requests in parallel to finish sooner.
Submit the tickets through the Message Batches API.
Stream each response, so the report can start building as results arrive.
Use fast mode on the synchronous API so the job finishes overnight.

explanation.correct: The Message Batches API costs 50% less and suits work nobody is waiting on. Most batches finish within an hour, and results are available within 24 hours, well before Monday morning.

distractors.A: Parallel synchronous calls finish sooner but pay full price for work that has no latency need.
distractors.C: Streaming helps interactive latency, not cost, and batches do not support it.
distractors.D: Fast mode tunes synchronous latency, which does not apply to batches.

questions.hint: Error propagation needs logging - track where failures occur.

questions.scenario: A script submits 5,000 documents as one batch and then pairs results with inputs by position: the first result goes with the first document, and so on. Spot checks show many labels attached to the wrong documents.
questions.question: What is the fix?

options.text: Sort the results by creation time before pairing them with the inputs.
Submit each document as its own batch so that ordering cannot matter.
Give each request a custom_id, and match results by that ID.
Use smaller batches of 100, which keep results in the original order.

explanation.correct: Batch results can come back in any order. Each request carries a custom_id, and the result for it carries the same ID, which is the only reliable way to pair them.

distractors.A: Results have no ordering guarantee to restore, so sorting does not recover the pairing.
distractors.B: One batch per document throws away the batching benefits and adds overhead.
distractors.D: Order is not guaranteed at any batch size.

questions.hint: Message routing checks types correctly - validate input types.

questions.scenario: Documents arrive continuously and must be processed within 36 hours of arrival. The team wants the 50% batch discount, and plans for the worst case of a batch taking the full 24 hours to finish.
questions.question: How often should the team submit batches?

options.text: At least every 8 hours, leaving room under 36.
Once a day, at a fixed time every night.
Every 16 hours, to keep the number of batches low.
Every 36 hours, matching the SLA window.

explanation.correct: A document can wait up to one submission interval before it is batched, then up to 24 hours more. An 8-hour interval gives a worst case of 32 hours, inside the 36-hour SLA with margin.

distractors.B: Up to 24 hours of waiting plus 24 hours of processing is 48, past the SLA.
distractors.C: 16 plus 24 is 40 hours, past the SLA.
distractors.D: 36 plus 24 is 60 hours, far past the SLA.

questions.hint: Input validation catches missing fields - check required properties.

questions.scenario: A batch of 20,000 document summaries finishes with 600 errored results. The logs show most of those documents exceeded the context limit.
questions.question: What should the team do next?

options.text: Resubmit the whole batch of 20,000 so that every result comes from the same run.
Drop the 600 errored documents, since 97% of the work did succeed.
Resubmit the 600 failed requests unchanged in a new batch of their own.
Resubmit only the failed custom_ids, splitting oversized documents into chunks.

explanation.correct: Errored results can be identified by custom_id and resubmitted on their own. Because they failed for being too long, they need a change, such as chunking, before resubmission.

distractors.A: Reprocessing 19,400 successes wastes money and time.
distractors.B: Silently dropping 3% of documents leaves gaps in the output.
distractors.C: Resubmitting unchanged repeats the same context-limit failure.

questions.hint: Tool response design affects Claude's next steps - structure outputs clearly.

questions.scenario: A team wants to move a nightly enrichment job to the Message Batches API. Today, Claude calls the team's own lookup_account tool in the middle of each request and uses the result to write a summary.
questions.question: How should they design the batch job?

options.text: Keep the tool. The Batches API calls the team's tool endpoint mid-request.
Prefetch each account's data into that request's prompt.
Stay on the synchronous API, since batches cannot handle anything with tools.
Add server-side fallbacks so that requests needing the tool can still finish.

explanation.correct: Each batch request runs independently, and nothing executes your own tools for you mid-request. A request that stops on a tool_use block would need another round. Fetching the data up front makes each request self-contained, so it works in one pass.

distractors.A: The API never calls your endpoints. Client tools are executed by your code, which is not in the loop during a batch.
distractors.C: Batches do accept tool definitions and server tools. Staying synchronous gives up the discount when prefetching solves the problem.
distractors.D: Fallbacks are not supported in batches, and they handle refusals, not tool calls.

questions.hint: Error categorization enables proper response - don't treat all same.

questions.scenario: A team is about to batch-process 200,000 contracts with a new extraction prompt. If the prompt has a flaw, they will pay for 200,000 bad results and wait up to a day to find out.
questions.question: What should they do first?

options.text: Submit everything now and fix any problems in a second full batch afterwards.
Split the work into two batches of 100,000 and refine the prompt between them.
Test and refine the prompt on a representative sample before the full batch.
Submit everything with max_tokens set as high as possible to avoid failures.

explanation.correct: Refining the prompt on a small, representative sample catches problems cheaply and quickly, which maximizes first-pass success when the large batch runs.

distractors.A: A flawed prompt then costs a full extra batch plus a day of waiting.
distractors.B: Half the contracts still run on an untested prompt.
distractors.D: A higher token limit does not fix a flawed prompt.

questions.hint: File name patterns help Claude find right files - use consistent naming.

questions.scenario: A legal team reviews contract bundles: a master agreement plus six schedules, about 120 pages in all. A single review pass catches problems within each document but often misses conflicts between documents, such as a payment term in Schedule C that contradicts the master agreement.
questions.question: How should the review be structured?

options.text: Review each document separately, then run a consistency pass.
Keep one pass, but list the schedules in priority order at the top of the prompt.
Have the owner of each schedule review their own schedule manually instead.
Summarize every document first, then review the short summaries together.

explanation.correct: Focused passes give each document full attention for local issues, and a separate pass dedicated to cross-document consistency looks specifically for contradictions between them.

distractors.B: Reordering the inputs does not give cross-document conflicts dedicated attention.
distractors.C: Individual owners see only their own schedule, which is exactly how cross-document conflicts slip through.
distractors.D: Summaries drop the precise terms, such as dates and amounts, where conflicts hide.

questions.hint: Edit tool requires exact file matching - ensure IDs are unique.

questions.scenario: An automated reviewer produces about 500 findings a day, and the human reviewers can check only about 100. Right now they check them in the order they arrive.
questions.question: How should findings be routed to reviewers?

options.text: Pick a random 100 findings each day, so that every finding has a fair chance.
Check the 100 oldest findings first, so that none of them waits too long.
Trust all high-confidence findings automatically, and review none of them.
Calibrate model confidence on labeled data; route low ones to humans.

explanation.correct: Per-finding confidence becomes useful for routing once its thresholds are calibrated against labeled examples. Then limited reviewer time goes to the findings most likely to be wrong.

distractors.A: Random selection ignores which findings most need a human.
distractors.B: Age says nothing about which findings are risky.
distractors.C: Auto-trusting high confidence without calibration or spot checks lets confident errors through.

questions.hint: Context tracking helps Claude build correct responses - maintain state.

questions.scenario: A coding agent writes SQL migrations. Afterwards, the same session is asked to review its own migration with high reasoning effort, and it approves migrations that later lock large tables in production. An engineer proposes raising effort to the maximum.
questions.question: What change will most improve the reviews?

options.text: Raise the reasoning effort for the review step to the maximum.
Ask the same session to list its assumptions before it reviews.
Review in a fresh instance given just the spec and migration.
Have the same session review the migration twice in a row.

explanation.correct: A model that keeps its generation context may repeat the same assumptions when it reviews its own work. An independent instance, given only the spec and the migration, reviews what was actually written.

distractors.A: More effort in the same context still reasons from the same assumptions.
distractors.B: Listing assumptions shows what the session already noticed, not what it missed.
distractors.D: Repeating the review in the same session repeats the same blind spots.

questions.hint: Result validation prevents errors from propagating - check as you go.

questions.scenario: A support agent summarizes older turns to keep long conversations within budget. In one case, "refund of $1,284.50 promised by June 3, order 77812" became "customer expects a refund soon" in the summary. Later, the agent could not confirm the amount or the date.
questions.question: What change prevents this?

options.text: Summarize less often, so that each summary has fewer turns to compress.
Keep a case-facts block of amounts, dates, and IDs outside the summary.
Ask the summarizer to be more detailed whenever it condenses the turns.
Stop summarizing, and always send every turn of the full history instead.

explanation.correct: Progressive summarization tends to blur exact values. Pulling transactional facts (amounts, dates, order numbers, commitments) into a persistent case-facts block that goes into every prompt keeps them exact, however the history is condensed.

distractors.A: Summarizing less often delays the loss of detail without preventing it.
distractors.C: "More detailed" is still a summary, and exact figures remain at risk.
distractors.D: Sending the full history works until the context fills up, which is why summarization was added.

sources: Design guidance, not a claim from Anthropic docs (checked 2026-11-07)
questions.hint: Synthesis groups findings by claim - organize evidence for clarity.

questions.scenario: An agent's order-lookup tool returns 45 fields per order, but the agent only ever uses five: status, items, delivery date, return window, and total. After about ten lookups the context is crowded, and response quality drops.
questions.question: What is the best change?

options.text: Move the agent to a model with a much larger context window.
Summarize the whole conversation every three turns to save room.
Tell the agent in its prompt to ignore fields that it does not need.
Trim each lookup to the needed fields before it enters context.

explanation.correct: Tool results accumulate in context and use tokens out of proportion to their relevance. Trimming each result to the fields the task needs, in the tool or in a post-processing step, keeps context for what matters.

distractors.A: A larger window postpones the problem while still paying for 40 unused fields per lookup.
distractors.B: Frequent summarization risks blurring the facts that do matter.
distractors.C: Ignored fields still take up space in context.

questions.hint: Claim status depends on value and date - maintain data quality.

questions.scenario: An analyst prompt starts with the question, followed by three 80-page financial filings pasted one after another without labels. Answers often miss details or attribute figures to the wrong company.
questions.question: How should the prompt be restructured?

options.text: Put tagged documents with sources first, and the question last.
Keep the question first, and repeat it again halfway through the filings.
Split the filings into pages and ask the question once for each page.
Shorten the question so that more of the context goes to the filings.

explanation.correct: For long inputs, documents placed at the top with the query at the end improve response quality, by up to 30% in Anthropic's tests. Wrapping each filing in document tags with its source keeps the companies apart.

distractors.B: Repeating the question does not fix the ordering or the unlabeled documents.
distractors.C: Page-by-page questions lose the cross-document context the analysis needs.
distractors.D: The question is not what crowds the context. Structure is the problem.

questions.hint: Gaps show where data is missing - report them explicitly.

questions.scenario: A coordinator concatenates twelve subagent reports and passes them to a synthesis step. The final summaries reliably include findings from the first and last reports, but often omit findings from reports in the middle.
questions.question: What change best addresses this?

options.text: Sort the twelve reports alphabetically by the subagent that wrote them.
Drop the middle reports, since they are the ones that keep getting missed.
Open with a key-findings summary, and give each report its own header.
Repeat the synthesis instruction once more at the end of the input.

explanation.correct: Material in the middle of a long input is easier to miss than material at either end. Leading with a summary of key findings from every report, and organizing the details under clear section headers, counters that position effect.

distractors.A: Alphabetical order just changes which reports end up in the middle.
distractors.B: Dropping reports loses findings deliberately.
distractors.D: Repeating the instruction does not give the middle reports more weight.

questions.hint: Route contradictory evidence to human review - flag for experts.

questions.scenario: To save tokens, a chat backend sends Claude only the newest user message plus a one-line summary of the previous reply. Users complain that the assistant asks for details they already gave and contradicts earlier answers.
questions.question: What is the right fix?

options.text: Pass a session ID, so the API recalls earlier turns from its own memory.
Send the full conversation each time, and use prompt caching for cost.
Send the last two turns, plus the one-line summary of everything earlier.
Store the conversation with Anthropic by putting a user ID in metadata.

explanation.correct: The Messages API is stateless: it knows only what each request contains. Coherence needs the full history in every request, and prompt caching makes the repeated prefix cheap.

distractors.A: The Messages API does not remember earlier requests by any ID.
distractors.C: Two turns plus a one-line summary still drops details users already gave.
distractors.D: Metadata does not store or replay conversation history.

questions.hint: Low confidence fields need human attention - don't guess.

questions.scenario: A synthesis agent has a tight context budget. It receives six upstream analyses, each several thousand words long, mostly step-by-step reasoning with the conclusions buried at the end. The synthesis often overflows its budget or misses key points.
questions.question: What change works best?

options.text: Cut each analysis down to its first 2,000 tokens before synthesis.
Give the synthesis agent a bigger model with a larger context window.
Tell the synthesis agent to skim each analysis for its main points.
Have upstream agents return key facts, citations, and relevance only.

explanation.correct: When the consumer has a limited budget, the producers should change their output. Structured key facts with citations and relevance scores carry the signal without the reasoning chains.

distractors.A: Truncation keeps the reasoning and drops the conclusions at the end, the reverse of what is needed.
distractors.B: A bigger window still pays for verbose content and does not surface the conclusions.
distractors.C: Skimming is unreliable and still loads all the text into context.

questions.hint: Stratified sampling from each stratum - ensure coverage.

questions.scenario: Over a 40-turn chat, a customer raises three separate problems: a damaged item (order A-102), a double charge (order B-311), and a delayed delivery (order C-047). By the end, the agent mixes up which order ID goes with which problem.
questions.question: What design best prevents the mix-ups?

options.text: Ask the customer to restate every order ID whenever it is needed again.
Keep the full chat history, and tell the agent to read it all carefully.
Keep a separate record per issue (order ID, amount, status) in context.
Split the conversation into three chats, each with its own agent.

explanation.correct: Pulling each issue into its own structured record, outside the free-flowing history, gives the agent an exact, per-issue reference that does not blur as the conversation grows.

distractors.A: Asking customers to repeat themselves is poor service, and the agent can still mismatch the answers.
distractors.B: Careful reading of 40 turns is exactly where the mix-ups happen.
distractors.D: Splitting the chat breaks a single conversation and loses context the issues share.

questions.hint: Never duplicate IDs in samples - track what you've seen.

questions.scenario: Partway through a chat, a customer writes: "I'd like to speak to a person, please." Their issue is a simple address change the agent could complete itself. The agent replies by asking a troubleshooting question first.
questions.question: What should the agent do?

options.text: Honor the request and hand off to a person right away.
Make the address change first, then offer a person.
Ask the customer why they would prefer to speak to a person.
Hand off only if the customer seems upset in tone.

explanation.correct: An explicit request for a human should be honored immediately, without first attempting the investigation or fix. Being able to solve the issue does not override the customer's stated choice.

distractors.B: Doing the work first delays what the customer asked for.
distractors.C: Questioning the request adds friction when the preference is already clear.
distractors.D: An explicit request does not depend on tone.

questions.hint: Provenance review traces data back to sources - document chain.

questions.scenario: A customer writes angrily that their order is a week late. The policy clearly allows the agent to reship it at no charge. The customer has not asked for a human.
questions.question: What is the best response?

options.text: Escalate to a human at once, because the customer is clearly frustrated.
Process the reship without acknowledging how the customer is feeling.
Acknowledge the frustration, offer the reship, and escalate if they ask.
Offer a discount code first, to calm them down before handling it.

explanation.correct: Frustration alone is not an escalation trigger when the issue is within the agent's ability. Acknowledging the feeling and resolving the problem serves the customer. Escalation follows if they say they would rather talk to a person.

distractors.A: Escalating on sentiment sends solvable cases to humans and delays the fix.
distractors.B: Ignoring the frustration makes a correct fix feel dismissive.
distractors.D: A discount is not a substitute for solving the late order.

questions.hint: Claim status needs both value and date - temporal context matters.

questions.scenario: A customer asks the agent to match a lower price they found on a competitor's website. The written policy covers price adjustments only when the company's own site lowers a price, and says nothing about competitor prices.
questions.question: What should the agent do?

options.text: Apply the own-site price-adjustment policy, by analogy, to the competitor.
Escalate, because the policy does not cover competitor price matching.
Refuse outright, since the competitor case is not listed in the policy.
Match the price anyway, since keeping the customer happy comes first.

explanation.correct: When policy is silent or ambiguous about the specific request, the decision belongs to someone with authority to set it. Escalating avoids inventing policy in either direction.

distractors.A: Extending a policy by analogy makes a decision the business has not made.
distractors.C: A flat refusal also invents policy, just in the other direction.
distractors.D: Matching without authority creates commitments the business may not honor.

questions.hint: Gap detection compares expected vs actual data - be thorough.

questions.scenario: A customer gives the name "J. Smith." The lookup tool returns three customer records with that name, each with different recent orders.
questions.question: How should the agent proceed?

options.text: Pick the record whose account had activity most recently.
Pick the record that has the largest number of orders on file.
Proceed with all three records until the right one becomes clear.
Ask for another identifier, such as an email or an order number.

explanation.correct: Multiple matches call for clarification, not a guess. Asking for a distinguishing identifier picks the right account before anything is read or changed.

distractors.A: Recency is a guess that can expose or change someone else's account.
distractors.B: Order count is also a guess, with the same risk.
distractors.C: Acting on all three mixes up accounts and may leak details between customers.

questions.hint: Contradictory evidence routing needs confidence thresholds.

questions.scenario: An agent spends nine turns trying different tools on a corrupted account record. Every attempt fails in a new way, and the customer has waited ten minutes. The agent never escalates, because its prompt lists escalation only for customer requests and refunds over $500.
questions.question: What change best fixes this?

options.text: Raise the turn limit, so the agent has more chances to find a fix.
Escalate after any single tool error, so that no customer is kept waiting.
Add "no meaningful progress" as a trigger, with a structured handoff.
Let the agent keep trying, since persistence usually solves it eventually.

explanation.correct: Inability to make progress is a standard escalation trigger alongside explicit requests and policy gaps. Adding it, with a handoff summary of what was tried, gets the customer to someone who can fix the record.

distractors.A: More turns prolong a failing approach while the customer waits.
distractors.B: Escalating on the first error sends recoverable problems to humans.
distractors.D: Nine distinct failures show this is not going to resolve itself.

questions.hint: Low confidence needs either uncertainty or conflict handling.

questions.scenario: A research system has four source subagents. The one covering academic journals fails because of a paywall, while the other three succeed. The coordinator must deliver a report today.
questions.question: How should the final report handle this?

options.text: Deliver it, noting what's well supported and which sources were missing.
Deliver it without mentioning the missing source, since three of four succeeded.
Hold the report until the journal source succeeds, however long that takes.
Fill the journal gap from the model's general knowledge of the field.

explanation.correct: Coverage annotations tell readers which findings are well supported and which areas have gaps because a source was unavailable. The report ships on time, and nobody mistakes partial coverage for complete coverage.

distractors.B: Hiding the gap overstates how complete the research is.
distractors.C: Waiting indefinitely misses the deadline for a gap that can be disclosed.

questions.scenario: A pipeline analyzes 20 documents in parallel subagents. When one analyzer throws an exception, the whole run aborts and the 19 completed analyses are discarded. Reruns are expensive.
questions.question: What is the better design?

options.text: Retry the entire pipeline automatically whenever any one analyzer fails.
Keep the 19 analyses; report the failed one with its error context.
Mark the whole run as successful, and quietly skip the document that failed.
Raise the analyzer timeout so that failures become much less likely to occur.

explanation.correct: Ending an entire workflow because of one failure throws away good work. Isolating the failure, keeping the completed results, and reporting the failed document with its context lets the coordinator decide whether to retry, substitute, or proceed.

distractors.A: Rerunning everything repeats 19 successful, expensive analyses.
distractors.C: Hiding the failure produces a result that looks complete but is not.
distractors.D: Timeouts are only one failure type, and the abort-everything design remains.

questions.scenario: Transient errors are retried in three places: the tool wrapper retries 3 times, the subagent retries 3 times, and the coordinator retries 3 times. During a short outage, one failing call turns into 27 attempts, and the burst makes the outage worse.
questions.question: What is the best fix?

options.text: Add exponential backoff at all three layers, but keep each layer's retries.
Retry once, near the failure; layers above pass it on and don't retry.
Remove retries everywhere, and report every transient error to a person.
Increase the coordinator's retries, so it can recover from more outages.

explanation.correct: Retries at several layers multiply. Handling transient errors in one bounded place, close to where they happen, with the layers above propagating the structured error instead of retrying, keeps recovery without the storm.

distractors.A: Backoff spreads the attempts out over time, but 3 × 3 × 3 is still 27 attempts.
distractors.C: Dropping retries entirely turns every brief blip into a human escalation.
distractors.D: More coordinator retries multiply the storm further.

questions.scenario: Two hours into exploring a large codebase, Claude starts answering with "typically, services like this would..." instead of naming the specific classes and files it found earlier in the session.
questions.question: What practice best prevents this drift?

options.text: Restart the session from scratch every hour, whatever the progress.
Ask Claude to try harder to remember what it found earlier on.
Keep a scratchpad file of key findings and have Claude consult it.
Raise max_tokens so Claude has more room for longer answers.

explanation.correct: In long sessions, context degrades and answers drift toward generic patterns. A scratchpad file of key findings (class names, file paths, decisions) persists outside the context and gives Claude a specific reference to consult.

distractors.A: Restarting without carrying findings forward loses the work.
distractors.B: Asking to remember better does not counter context degradation.
distractors.D: max_tokens limits output length, not what Claude retains.

questions.scenario: An investigation runs in phases. In phase 1, subagents mapped the payment modules and their owners. In phase 2, new subagents must trace specific bugs through those modules. Each phase-2 subagent currently rediscovers the module layout from scratch.

options.text: Pass a summary of phase-1 findings in each phase-2 prompt.
Let every phase-2 subagent rediscover the layout, so its picture is current.
Pass the entire phase-1 transcript into each of the phase-2 subagent prompts.
Run phase 2 in the main context, so it can see the phase-1 work directly.

explanation.correct: Subagents start without the parent's history, so the earlier phase's findings must be passed in their prompts. A concise summary of what phase 1 established gives each phase-2 subagent the map without the noise.

questions.scenario: A three-hour multi-agent analysis crashed at the two-hour mark. Rerunning it started from zero, because nothing about each agent's progress had been saved anywhere outside the processes.
questions.question: What design makes the next crash recoverable?

options.text: Break all analyses into tasks short enough to finish before any crash.
Rely on resuming the coordinator's session to bring back everything else.
Rerun the full analysis nightly so that a fresh result is always ready.
Have agents export state to a known location; resume from a manifest.

explanation.correct: Structured state persistence makes progress survive a crash: each agent writes its state to a known location, and on restart the coordinator loads a manifest and injects each agent's saved state into its prompt, so work continues where it stopped.

distractors.C: Nightly reruns throw away the partial work and only shift the timing.

questions.scenario: Deep into a debugging session, the context is filling with verbose search output. The developer wants to keep going in the same session without losing the thread.
questions.question: What is the best move?

options.text: Run /clear, then explain the problem again to Claude from the beginning.
Run /compact, and keep any rules that must always hold in CLAUDE.md.
Quit, and start a brand-new session with no summary of the work so far.
Keep going until the session runs out of context, then deal with it.

explanation.correct: /compact summarizes older history to free space while keeping the thread. Compaction can drop specific early instructions, so rules that must persist belong in CLAUDE.md, which is re-injected on every request.

distractors.A: /clear empties the context, so the developer has to rebuild everything by hand.
distractors.C: A fresh session without a summary loses the progress made so far.
distractors.D: Waiting until the context is full risks an abrupt cut-off at a worse moment.

questions.scenario: Early in a long session, a developer told Claude: "Never modify files under generated/." Hours later, after automatic compaction, Claude edited a file in generated/. The developer proposes turning compaction off.
questions.question: What is the best fix?

options.text: Repeat the instruction in the chat every few turns from now on.
Turn off compaction, so early instructions are never summarized.
Move the rule to CLAUDE.md; add a hook if it must never break.
Switch to a model with a larger context window to delay compaction.

explanation.correct: Compaction replaces older messages with a summary, so specific early instructions may not survive. CLAUDE.md is re-injected on every request, which makes it the place for persistent rules. A PreToolUse hook makes the rule deterministic if it must hold every time.

distractors.A: Manual repetition is fragile and depends on the developer remembering.
distractors.B: Without compaction, long sessions hit the context limit and fail.
distractors.D: A larger window postpones compaction but does not prevent it.

questions.scenario: An extraction system is 97% accurate overall, and management wants to remove human review. Typed invoices make up 85% of the volume. A spot check suggests handwritten receipts may be much less accurate.
questions.question: What should the team do before reducing review?

options.text: Measure accuracy by document type and field before automating.
Automate everything, since 97% overall accuracy is well above the target.
Raise the overall accuracy target to 99%, and then automate everything.
Collect more data across the board, then recompute the overall figure.

explanation.correct: Aggregate accuracy can hide poor performance in specific document types or fields. Validating each segment first shows which ones are safe to automate, perhaps typed invoices, and which still need people.

distractors.B: The high overall figure is driven by the 85% of typed invoices and can mask weak receipt accuracy.
distractors.C: A higher aggregate target still hides how each segment performs.
distractors.D: More data recomputes the same blended number without breaking it down.

questions.scenario: High-confidence extractions now skip human review. The team needs to keep measuring the error rate on those automated extractions and to notice new kinds of errors as document formats change.
questions.question: Which review strategy fits?

options.text: Review none of the high-confidence items, since that is why they were automated.
Review only the high-confidence items that customers complain about later.
Review the 10 most recent high-confidence items at the end of each day.
Review a stratified random sample of them, spread across types and fields.

explanation.correct: Stratified random sampling of automated, high-confidence items measures the ongoing error rate fairly across segments and surfaces new error patterns before they spread.

distractors.A: With no review, rising error rates and new failure patterns go unseen.
distractors.B: Complaints arrive late and represent only the errors customers happen to notice.
distractors.C: The most recent items are not a representative sample.

questions.scenario: An extraction pipeline sees a contract that lists two different effective dates in two clauses. Its confidence score for the date field is moderate.
questions.question: How should the pipeline handle this document?

options.text: Pick the date that appears first in the contract, and continue.
Send it to human review, noting the contradictory dates.
Take the later date, since amendments usually come at the end.
Leave the date field empty, and continue without saying anything.

explanation.correct: Contradictory source documents and low or moderate confidence are what limited reviewer time should go to. Routing the document to a person, with the conflict noted, puts it where human judgment is needed.

distractors.A: Picking the first date is a guess on a legally significant field.
distractors.C: The "later is newer" rule is also a guess that may be wrong for this contract.
distractors.D: Silently leaving the field empty hides the conflict instead of resolving it.

questions.scenario: An extraction model outputs a confidence score for each field. The team set one threshold of 0.9 for every field, chosen because it "feels high". Audits show that 0.9 is very reliable for invoice numbers but often wrong for line-item descriptions.
questions.question: What is the best way to set the thresholds?

options.text: Keep 0.9 for every field, because a high threshold should be safe enough.
Average each document's field confidences and apply 0.9 to that average.
Calibrate a separate threshold for each field against a labeled set.
Trust the model's scores directly, since it knows its own reliability.

explanation.correct: Raw confidence scores are not calibrated, and their meaning differs by field. Measuring actual accuracy at each score on a labeled validation set, field by field, shows where each threshold must sit to achieve the target accuracy.

distractors.A: One uncalibrated threshold is too strict for some fields and too loose for others, which the audit already shows.
distractors.B: Averaging hides the weak fields behind the strong ones.
distractors.D: Self-reported confidence is not reliable without calibration.

questions.scenario: Research subagents send findings to a synthesis agent as plain summaries. The final report makes strong claims, but reviewers often cannot tell which source supports which claim.
questions.question: What change best preserves provenance?

options.text: Ask the synthesis agent to add citations at the end, from memory.
Add a bibliography listing every source the subagents consulted.
Have reviewers search for a source for each claim in the report.
Have subagents send claim-source mappings that synthesis keeps.

explanation.correct: Attribution is lost when findings are compressed without their sources. Structured claim-source mappings (source URL, document name, relevant excerpt), which synthesis must keep and merge, carry the attribution through to the report.

distractors.A: Citations added from memory after the fact are unreliable and can be fabricated.
distractors.B: A flat bibliography does not say which source supports which claim.
distractors.C: Reconstructing sources by hand is slow and may find different sources than the ones used.

questions.scenario: Two credible sources report different figures for the same market statistic, 23% and 31%. The synthesis agent picked 31% without comment, and a reader later found the other source.
questions.question: How should conflicting figures be handled?

options.text: Report both figures with their sources, and say that they conflict.
Average the two figures and report 27% as the market statistic.
Use the more recently published figure, and do not mention the other.
Leave the statistic out of the report, since its value is uncertain.

explanation.correct: When credible sources disagree, the honest output preserves both values with attribution and flags the conflict. The analysis step should pass both figures along, so the coordinator or reader can decide how to reconcile them.

distractors.B: An average is a number no source reported.
distractors.C: Recency may matter, but silently dropping a credible figure hides the disagreement.
distractors.D: Omitting the statistic withholds relevant, if contested, information.
